### Load CSV, JSONL, Parquet, and Excel files from filesystem to DuckDB with dlt

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/filesystem-local/load-data-with-python-from-filesystem-local-to-duckdb

This is the main example from the page, showing how to load CSV files from a filesystem into DuckDB using the dlt readers resource. It includes multiple functions: read_csv_with_duckdb, read_csv_duckdb_compressed, read_parquet_and_jsonl_chunked, read_custom_file_type_excel, and copy_files_resource. The code demonstrates merging on a date key, reading compressed files, reading JSONL and Parquet in chunks, using a custom transformer for Excel files, and copying files locally with fsspec.

```python
    # load all csvs in A801
    met_files = readers(
        bucket_url=TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="met_csv/A801/*.csv"
    ).read_csv()
    # tell dlt to merge on date
    met_files.apply_hints(write_disposition="merge", merge_key="date")
    # NOTE: we load to met_csv table
    load_info = pipeline.run(met_files.with_name("met_csv"))
    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)

    # now let's simulate loading on next day. not only current data appears but also updated record for the previous day are present
    # all the records for previous day will be replaced with new records
    met_files = readers(
        bucket_url=TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="met_csv/A801/*.csv"
    ).read_csv()
    met_files.apply_hints(write_disposition="merge", merge_key="date")
    load_info = pipeline.run(met_files.with_name("met_csv"))

    # you can also do dlt pipeline standard_filesystem_csv show to confirm that all A801 were replaced with A803 records for overlapping day
    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)


def read_csv_with_duckdb() -> None:
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="standard_filesystem",
        destination='duckdb',
        dataset_name="met_data_duckdb",
    )

    # load all the CSV data, excluding headers
    met_files = readers(
        bucket_url=TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="met_csv/A801/*.csv"
    ).read_csv_duckdb(chunk_size=1000, header=True)

    load_info = pipeline.run(met_files)

    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)


def read_csv_duckdb_compressed() -> None:
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="standard_filesystem",
        destination='duckdb',
        dataset_name="taxi_data",
        full_refresh=True,
    )

    met_files = readers(
        bucket_url=TESTS_BUCKET_URL,
        file_glob="gzip/*",
    ).read_csv_duckdb()

    load_info = pipeline.run(met_files)
    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)


def read_parquet_and_jsonl_chunked() -> None:
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="standard_filesystem",
        destination='duckdb',
        dataset_name="teams_data",
    )
    # When using the readers resource, you can specify a filter to select only the files you
    # want to load including a glob pattern. If you use a recursive glob pattern, the filenames
    # will include the path to the file inside the bucket_url.

    # JSONL reading (in large chunks!)
    jsonl_reader = readers(TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="**/*.jsonl").read_jsonl(
        chunksize=10000
    )
    # PARQUET reading
    parquet_reader = readers(TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="**/*.parquet").read_parquet()
    # load both folders together to specified tables
    load_info = pipeline.run(
        [
            jsonl_reader.with_name("jsonl_team_data"),
            parquet_reader.with_name("parquet_team_data"),
        ]
    )
    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)


def read_custom_file_type_excel() -> None:
    """Here we create an extract pipeline using filesystem resource and read_csv transformer"""

    # instantiate filesystem directly to get list of files (FileItems) and then use read_excel transformer to get
    # content of excel via pandas

    @dlt.transformer(standalone=True)
    def read_excel(
        items: Iterator[FileItemDict], sheet_name: str
    ) -> Iterator[TDataItems]:
        import pandas as pd

        for file_obj in items:
            with file_obj.open() as file:
                yield pd.read_excel(file, sheet_name).to_dict(orient="records")

    freshman_xls = filesystem(
        bucket_url=TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="../custom/freshman_kgs.xlsx"
    ) | read_excel("freshman_table")

    load_info = dlt.run(
        freshman_xls.with_name("freshman"),
        destination='duckdb',
        dataset_name="freshman_data",
    )
    print(load_info)


def copy_files_resource(local_folder: str) -> None:
    """Demonstrates how to copy files locally by adding a step to filesystem resource and the to load the download listing to db"""
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="standard_filesystem_copy",
        destination='duckdb',
        dataset_name="standard_filesystem_data",
    )

    # a step that copies files into test storage
    def _copy(item: FileItemDict) -> FileItemDict:
        # instantiate fsspec and copy file
        dest_file = os.path.join(local_folder, item["relative_path"])
        # create dest folder
        os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(dest_file), exist_ok=True)
        # download file
        item.fsspec.download(item["file_url"], dest_file)
```

### Override DuckLake data path with override_data_path

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/dlt-ecosystem/destinations/ducklake.md

Override the stored DATA_PATH in the DuckLake catalog with the current connection's DATA_PATH for reads and writes. The catalog's stored value is not modified. Useful when uploading a locally populated catalog and data to remote storage or accessing the same catalog from different environments. Can also be set via the environment variable DESTINATION__DUCKLAKE__OVERRIDE_DATA_PATH=true.

```toml
[destination.ducklake]
override_data_path=true
```

```python
import dlt
from dlt.destinations.impl.ducklake.configuration import DuckLakeCredentials

destination = dlt.destinations.ducklake(
    credentials=DuckLakeCredentials(
        catalog="sqlite:///catalog.sqlite",
        storage="s3://new-bucket/data",
    ),
    override_data_path=True,
)
```

### Simple custom destination function with @dlt.destination

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/dlt-ecosystem/destinations/destination.md

A minimal example of a custom destination function that prints table name and items. The function receives items and table schema, and is used as the destination for a pipeline.

```python
import dlt
from dlt.common.typing import TDataItems
from dlt.common.schema import TTableSchema

@dlt.destination(batch_size=10)
def my_destination(items: TDataItems, table: TTableSchema) -> None:
    print(table["name"])
    print(items)

pipeline = dlt.pipeline("custom_destination_pipeline", destination=my_destination)
pipeline.run([1, 2, 3], table_name="items")
```

### Quick example: RESTClient paginate() with dlt pipeline

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/dlt-ecosystem/verified-sources/rest_api/advanced.md

A simple dlt pipeline that reads issues from the GitHub API using RESTClient. The paginate() method automatically handles pagination and yields PageData objects. The pipeline loads the data into a DuckDB destination.

```python
import dlt
from dlt.sources.helpers.rest_client import RESTClient

github_client = RESTClient(base_url="https://api.github.com")  # (1)

@dlt.resource
def get_issues():
    for page in github_client.paginate(                        # (2)
        "/repos/dlt-hub/dlt/issues",                           # (3)
        params={                                               # (4)
            "per_page": 100,
            "sort": "updated",
            "direction": "desc",
        },
    ):
        yield page                                             # (5)


pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
    pipeline_name="github_issues",
    destination="duckdb",
    dataset_name="github_data",
)
load_info = pipeline.run(get_issues)
print(load_info)

### Run dlt pipeline for GitHub data to AlloyDB

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/github/load-data-with-python-from-github-to-alloydb

The main pipeline script generated by the dlt CLI at github_pipeline.py. It defines three load functions: load_duckdb_repo_reactions_issues_only (loads only issues for duckdb/duckdb with items_per_page=100 and max_items=100), load_airflow_events (loads apache/airflow events with an empty access_token to force anonymous access and demonstrates incremental loading), and load_dlthub_dlt_all_data (loads all issues, pull requests, and comments for dlt-hub/dlt). All pipelines use destination='postgres' and print the pipeline.run(data) result.

```python
import dlt

from github import github_reactions, github_repo_events


def load_duckdb_repo_reactions_issues_only() -> None:
    """Loads issues, their comments and reactions for duckdb"""
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        "github_reactions",
        destination='postgres',
        dataset_name="duckdb_issues",
        full_refresh=True,
    )
    # get only 100 items (for issues and pull request)
    data = github_reactions(
        "duckdb", "duckdb", items_per_page=100, max_items=100
    ).with_resources("issues")
    print(pipeline.run(data))


def load_airflow_events() -> None:
    """Loads airflow events. Shows incremental loading. Forces anonymous access token"""
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        "github_events", destination='postgres', dataset_name="airflow_events"
    )
    data = github_repo_events("apache", "airflow", access_token="")
    print(pipeline.run(data))
    # if you uncomment this, it does not load the same events again
    # data = github_repo_events("apache", "airflow", access_token="")
    # print(pipeline.run(data))


def load_dlthub_dlt_all_data() -> None:
    """Loads all issues, pull requests and comments for dlthub dlt repo"""
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        "github_reactions",
        destination='postgres',
        dataset_name="dlthub_reactions",
        full_refresh=True,
    )
    data = github_reactions("dlt-hub", "dlt")
    print(pipeline.run(data))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    load_duckdb_repo_reactions_issues_only()
    load_airflow_events()
    load_dlthub_dlt_all_data()

```

### dlt pipeline examples: CSV merge, DuckDB, JSONL/Parquet, Excel, copy

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/filesystem/load-data-with-python-from-filesystem-to-filesystem-local

Python functions demonstrating dlt pipeline runs from a local filesystem bucket to a filesystem destination. Covers CSV merging on a date column, DuckDB-backed CSV reading (including gzip), chunked JSONL and Parquet loading, a custom Excel transformer, and a local file copy step. Requires the dlt library and a local test bucket path.

```python
TESTS_BUCKET_URL = posixpath.abspath("../tests/filesystem/samples/")


def stream_and_merge_csv() -> None:
    """Demonstrates how to scan folder with csv files, load them in chunk and merge on date column with the previous load"""
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="standard_filesystem_csv",
        destination='filesystem',
        dataset_name="met_data",
    )
    # met_data contains 3 columns, where "date" column contain a date on which we want to merge
    # load all csvs in A801
    met_files = readers(
        bucket_url=TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="met_csv/A801/*.csv"
    ).read_csv()
    # tell dlt to merge on date
    met_files.apply_hints(write_disposition="merge", merge_key="date")
    # NOTE: we load to met_csv table
    load_info = pipeline.run(met_files.with_name("met_csv"))
    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)

    # now let's simulate loading on next day. not only current data appears but also updated record for the previous day are present
    # all the records for previous day will be replaced with new records
    met_files = readers(
        bucket_url=TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="met_csv/A801/*.csv"
    ).read_csv()
    met_files.apply_hints(write_disposition="merge", merge_key="date")
    load_info = pipeline.run(met_files.with_name("met_csv"))

    # you can also do dlt pipeline standard_filesystem_csv show to confirm that all A801 were replaced with A803 records for overlapping day
    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)


def read_csv_with_duckdb() -> None:
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="standard_filesystem",
        destination='filesystem',
        dataset_name="met_data_duckdb",
    )

    # load all the CSV data, excluding headers
    met_files = readers(
        bucket_url=TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="met_csv/A801/*.csv"
    ).read_csv_duckdb(chunk_size=1000, header=True)

    load_info = pipeline.run(met_files)

    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)


def read_csv_duckdb_compressed() -> None:
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="standard_filesystem",
        destination='filesystem',
        dataset_name="taxi_data",
        full_refresh=True,
    )

    met_files = readers(
        bucket_url=TESTS_BUCKET_URL,
        file_glob="gzip/*",
    ).read_csv_duckdb()

    load_info = pipeline.run(met_files)
    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)


def read_parquet_and_jsonl_chunked() -> None:
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="standard_filesystem",
        destination='filesystem',
        dataset_name="teams_data",
    )
    # When using the readers resource, you can specify a filter to select only the files you
    # want to load including a glob pattern. If you use a recursive glob pattern, the filenames
    # will include the path to the file inside the bucket_url.

    # JSONL reading (in large chunks!)
    jsonl_reader = readers(TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="**/*.jsonl").read_jsonl(
        chunksize=10000
    )
    # PARQUET reading
    parquet_reader = readers(TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="**/*.parquet").read_parquet()
    # load both folders together to specified tables
    load_info = pipeline.run(
        [
            jsonl_reader.with_name("jsonl_team_data"),
            parquet_reader.with_name("parquet_team_data"),
        ]
    )
    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)


def read_custom_file_type_excel() -> None:
    """Here we create an extract pipeline using filesystem resource and read_csv transformer"""

    # instantiate filesystem directly to get list of files (FileItems) and then use read_excel transformer to get
    # content of excel via pandas

    @dlt.transformer(standalone=True)
    def read_excel(
        items: Iterator[FileItemDict], sheet_name: str
    ) -> Iterator[TDataItems]:
        import pandas as pd

        for file_obj in items:
            with file_obj.open() as file:
                yield pd.read_excel(file, sheet_name).to_dict(orient="records")

    freshman_xls = filesystem(
        bucket_url=TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="../custom/freshman_kgs.xlsx"
    ) | read_excel("freshman_table")

    load_info = dlt.run(
        freshman_xls.with_name("freshman"),
        destination='filesystem',
        dataset_name="freshman_data",
    )
    print(load_info)

    """Demonstrates how to copy files locally by adding a step to filesystem resource and the to load the download listing to db"""
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(

### Python script for filesystem to filesystem pipeline

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/filesystem/load-data-with-python-from-filesystem-to-filesystem-gcs

This script defines a dlt pipeline that loads data from a filesystem source to a filesystem destination (GCS). It includes functions for copying files, streaming and merging CSV, reading parquet and JSONL, reading Excel, incremental loading, and using DuckDB. The main block runs all these functions.

```python
import os
import dlt
from dlt.sources.filesystem import filesystem, read_csv, read_parquet, read_jsonl, read_excel
from dlt.common.libs.deltalake import write_delta
from dlt.common.typing import FileItemDict

TESTS_BUCKET_URL = "gs://dlt-ci-test-bucket"


def copy_files_resource(local_folder: str) -> None:
    """
    Demonstrates how to copy files from a bucket to a local folder.
    """
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="standard_filesystem_copy",
        destination='filesystem',
        dataset_name="standard_filesystem_data",
    )

    # a step that copies files into test storage
    def _copy(item: FileItemDict) -> FileItemDict:
        # instantiate fsspec and copy file
        dest_file = os.path.join(local_folder, item["relative_path"])
        # create dest folder
        os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(dest_file), exist_ok=True)
        # download file
        item.fsspec.download(item["file_url"], dest_file)
        # return file item unchanged
        return item

    # use recursive glob pattern and add file copy step
    downloader = filesystem(TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="**").add_map(_copy)

    # NOTE: you do not need to load any data to execute extract, below we obtain
    # a list of files in a bucket and also copy them locally
    # listing = list(downloader)
    # print(listing)

    # download to table "listing"
    # downloader = filesystem(TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="**").add_map(_copy)
    load_info = pipeline.run(
        downloader.with_name("listing"), write_disposition="replace"
    )
    # pretty print the information on data that was loaded
    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)


def read_files_incrementally_mtime() -> None:
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="standard_filesystem_incremental",
        destination='filesystem',
        dataset_name="file_tracker",
    )

    # here we modify filesystem resource so it will track only new csv files
    # such resource may be then combined with transformer doing further processing
    new_files = filesystem(bucket_url=TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="csv/*")
    # add incremental on modification time
    new_files.apply_hints(incremental=dlt.sources.incremental("modification_date"))
    load_info = pipeline.run((new_files | read_csv()).with_name("csv_files"))
    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)

    # load again - no new files!
    new_files = filesystem(bucket_url=TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="csv/*")
    # add incremental on modification time
    new_files.apply_hints(incremental=dlt.sources.incremental("modification_date"))
    load_info = pipeline.run((new_files | read_csv()).with_name("csv_files"))
    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    copy_files_resource("_storage")
    stream_and_merge_csv()
    read_parquet_and_jsonl_chunked()
    read_custom_file_type_excel()
    read_files_incrementally_mtime()
    read_csv_with_duckdb()
    read_csv_duckdb_compressed()

```

### Load selected tables from MySQL to DuckDB with dlt

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/sql_database_hana/load-data-with-python-from-sql_database_hana-to-duckdb

Configures a dlt pipeline to load selected tables (family, genome) from the Rfam MySQL database into DuckDB using the pandas backend. The table adapter converts floats to decimals, and backend_kwargs set coerce_float to False and dtype_backend to numpy_nullable. The main block calls load_select_tables_from_database() and comments out alternative loading functions.

```python
destination='duckdb',
    dataset_name="rfam_data_pandas_2",
)

    def _double_as_decimal_adapter(table: sa.Table) -> None:
        """Emits decimals instead of floats."""
        for column in table.columns.values():
            if isinstance(column.type, sa.Float):
                column.type.asdecimal = True

    sql_alchemy_source = sql_database(
        "mysql+pymysql://rfamro@mysql-rfam-public.ebi.ac.uk:4497/Rfam?&binary_prefix=true",
        backend="pandas",
        table_adapter_callback=_double_as_decimal_adapter,
        chunk_size=100000,
        # set coerce_float to False to represent them as string
        backend_kwargs={"coerce_float": False, "dtype_backend": "numpy_nullable"},
        # preserve full typing info. this will parse
        detect_precision_hints=True,
    ).with_resources("family", "genome")

    info = pipeline.run(sql_alchemy_source)
    print(info)


if __name__ == "__main__":

### Declare destination and load with explicit bucket_url

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/general-usage/destination.md

Shows a multi-stage pipeline where extract and normalize do not need destination dependencies or credentials. The destination is accessed only when pipeline.load is called with an explicit filesystem destination and bucket_url.

```python
import dlt
from dlt.destinations import filesystem

# just declare the destination.
pipeline = dlt.pipeline("pipeline", destination="filesystem")
# no destination credentials not config needed to extract
pipeline.extract(["a", "b", "c"], table_name="letters")
# same to normalize
pipeline.normalize()
# here dependencies dependencies will be imported, secrets pulled and destination accessed
# we pass bucket_url explicitly and expect credentials passed by config provider
load_info = pipeline.load(destination=filesystem(bucket_url=bucket_url))
print(load_info)
```

### sync_destination

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/api_reference/dlt/pipeline

Synchronizes pipeline state with the destination's state kept in dataset_name. Attempts to restore pipeline state and schemas from the destination if the destination state has a higher version number.

```APIDOC
## sync_destination

### Description
Synchronizes pipeline state with the `destination`'s state kept in `dataset_name`. Attempts to restore pipeline state and schemas from the destination. Requires the state at the destination to have a higher version number than local state; otherwise, local state is replaced. If the dataset does not exist at the destination, local state is wiped.

### Method
sync_destination

### Signature
```
@with_config_section(sections=(), merge_func=ConfigSectionContext.prefer_existing)
def sync_destination(destination: TDestinationReferenceArg = None, staging: TDestinationReferenceArg = None, dataset_name: str = None) -> None
```

### Parameters
- **destination** (TDestinationReferenceArg) - Optional - Destination reference.
- **staging** (TDestinationReferenceArg) - Optional - Staging reference.
- **dataset_name** (str) - Optional - Name of the dataset at the destination.

### Returns
None

### Notes
- This method is executed by the `run` method before any operation on data. Use `restore_from_destination` configuration option to disable that behavior.
```

### Complete Python script for loading filesystem data with dlt

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/filesystem-aws/load-data-with-python-from-filesystem-aws-to-filesystem-gcs

This is the complete Python script from the documentation page. It demonstrates various ways to load data from a local filesystem into a dlt pipeline with destination 'filesystem'. It includes functions for streaming and merging CSV files, reading CSV with DuckDB (including compressed files), reading JSONL and Parquet files in chunks, and reading Excel files using a custom transformer.

```python
from dlt.sources import TDataItems

try:
    from .filesystem import FileItemDict, filesystem, readers, read_csv  # type: ignore
except ImportError:
    from filesystem import (
        FileItemDict,
        filesystem,
        readers,
        read_csv,
    )


TESTS_BUCKET_URL = posixpath.abspath("../tests/filesystem/samples/")


def stream_and_merge_csv() -> None:
    """Demonstrates how to scan folder with csv files, load them in chunk and merge on date column with the previous load"""
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="standard_filesystem_csv",
        destination='filesystem',
        dataset_name="met_data",
    )
    # met_data contains 3 columns, where "date" column contain a date on which we want to merge
    # load all csvs in A801
    met_files = readers(
        bucket_url=TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="met_csv/A801/*.csv"
    ).read_csv()
    # tell dlt to merge on date
    met_files.apply_hints(write_disposition="merge", merge_key="date")
    # NOTE: we load to met_csv table
    load_info = pipeline.run(met_files.with_name("met_csv"))
    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)

    # now let's simulate loading on next day. not only current data appears but also updated record for the previous day are present
    # all the records for previous day will be replaced with new records
    met_files = readers(
        bucket_url=TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="met_csv/A801/*.csv"
    ).read_csv()
    met_files.apply_hints(write_disposition="merge", merge_key="date")
    load_info = pipeline.run(met_files.with_name("met_csv"))

    # you can also do dlt pipeline standard_filesystem_csv show to confirm that all A801 were replaced with A803 records for overlapping day
    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)


def read_csv_with_duckdb() -> None:
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="standard_filesystem",
        destination='filesystem',
        dataset_name="met_data_duckdb",
    )

    # load all the CSV data, excluding headers
    met_files = readers(
        bucket_url=TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="met_csv/A801/*.csv"
    ).read_csv_duckdb(chunk_size=1000, header=True)

    load_info = pipeline.run(met_files)

    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)


def read_csv_duckdb_compressed() -> None:
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="standard_filesystem",
        destination='filesystem',
        dataset_name="taxi_data",
        full_refresh=True,
    )

    met_files = readers(
        bucket_url=TESTS_BUCKET_URL,
        file_glob="gzip/*",
    ).read_csv_duckdb()

    load_info = pipeline.run(met_files)
    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)


def read_parquet_and_jsonl_chunked() -> None:
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="standard_filesystem",
        destination='filesystem',
        dataset_name="teams_data",
    )
    # When using the readers resource, you can specify a filter to select only the files you
    # want to load including a glob pattern. If you use a recursive glob pattern, the filenames
    # will include the path to the file inside the bucket_url.

    # JSONL reading (in large chunks!)
    jsonl_reader = readers(TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="**/*.jsonl").read_jsonl(
        chunksize=10000
    )
    # PARQUET reading
    parquet_reader = readers(TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="**/*.parquet").read_parquet()
    # load both folders together to specified tables
    load_info = pipeline.run(
        [
            jsonl_reader.with_name("jsonl_team_data"),
            parquet_reader.with_name("parquet_team_data"),
        ]
    )
    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)


def read_custom_file_type_excel() -> None:
    """Here we create an extract pipeline using filesystem resource and read_csv transformer"""

    # instantiate filesystem directly to get list of files (FileItems) and then use read_excel transformer to get
    # content of excel via pandas

    @dlt.transformer(standalone=True)
    def read_excel(
        items: Iterator[FileItemDict], sheet_name: str
    ) -> Iterator[TDataItems]:
        import pandas as pd

        for file_obj in items:
            with file_obj.open() as file:
                yield pd.read_excel(file, sheet_name).to_dict(orient="records")

    freshman_xls = filesystem(
        bucket_url=TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="../custom/freshman_kgs.xlsx"
    ) | read_excel("freshman_table")

    load_info = dlt.run(
        freshman_xls.with_name("freshman"),
        destination='filesystem',
        dataset_name="freshman_data",
    )
```

### Python script for loading files from filesystem to MSSQL

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/filesystem/load-data-with-python-from-filesystem-to-mssql

This script defines multiple functions to load different file types from a filesystem to a Microsoft SQL Server destination using dlt. It includes functions for copying files, streaming and merging CSV, reading parquet and JSONL, reading Excel, incremental loading, and using DuckDB. The main block runs all these functions.

```python
    downloader = filesystem(TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="**").add_map(_copy)

    # NOTE: you do not need to load any data to execute extract, below we obtain
    # a list of files in a bucket and also copy them locally
    # listing = list(downloader)
    # print(listing)

    # download to table "listing"
    # downloader = filesystem(TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="**").add_map(_copy)
    load_info = pipeline.run(
        downloader.with_name("listing"), write_disposition="replace"
    )
    # pretty print the information on data that was loaded
    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)


def read_files_incrementally_mtime() -> None:
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="standard_filesystem_incremental",
        destination='mssql',
        dataset_name="file_tracker",
    )

    # here we modify filesystem resource so it will track only new csv files
    # such resource may be then combined with transformer doing further processing
    new_files = filesystem(bucket_url=TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="csv/*")
    # add incremental on modification time
    new_files.apply_hints(incremental=dlt.sources.incremental("modification_date"))
    load_info = pipeline.run((new_files | read_csv()).with_name("csv_files"))
    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)

    # load again - no new files!
    new_files = filesystem(bucket_url=TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="csv/*")
    # add incremental on modification time
    new_files.apply_hints(incremental=dlt.sources.incremental("modification_date"))
    load_info = pipeline.run((new_files | read_csv()).with_name("csv_files"))
    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    copy_files_resource("_storage")
    stream_and_merge_csv()
    read_parquet_and_jsonl_chunked()
    read_custom_file_type_excel()
    read_files_incrementally_mtime()
    read_csv_with_duckdb()
    read_csv_duckdb_compressed()

```

### Use custom naming conventions with dlt pipelines

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/examples/custom_naming.md

Full example showing how to use custom naming conventions with dlt. It creates a Postgres destination with the `sql_cs_latin2` naming convention (case-sensitive, allows UNICODE letters) and runs a pipeline with data containing umlauts, then queries the loaded table with quoted identifiers. It also runs a DuckDB pipeline using the `sql_ci_no_collision` naming convention (configured via config.toml) to avoid collisions between case-insensitive identifiers, and uses `normalize_table_identifier` to get the actual table names for DESCRIBE queries.

```python
import dlt

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # NOTE: ql_cs_latin2 is case sensitive and postgres accepts UNICODE letters in identifiers
    # create postgres destination with a custom naming convention. sql_cs_latin2 is an importable
    # module
    # import sql_cs_latin2  # is resolving in this context

    dest_ = dlt.destinations.postgres(naming_convention="sql_cs_latin2")

    # run a pipeline
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="sql_cs_latin2_pipeline",
        destination=dest_,
        dataset_name="example_data",
        dev_mode=True,
    )
    # Extract, normalize, and load the data
    load_info = pipeline.run([{"StÃ¼ckId": 1}], table_name="AusrÃ¼stung")
    print(load_info)
    with pipeline.sql_client() as client:
        # NOTE: we quote case sensitive identifers
        with client.execute_query('SELECT "StÃ¼ckId" FROM "AusrÃ¼stung"') as cur:
            print(cur.description)
            print(cur.fetchone())

    # sql_ci_no_collision (configured in config toml)
    # NOTE: pipeline with name `sql_ci_no_collision` will create default schema with the same name
    # so we are free to use it in config.toml to just affect this pipeline and leave the postgres pipeline as it is
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="sql_ci_no_collision",
        destination="duckdb",
        dataset_name="example_data",
        dev_mode=True,
    )
    # duckdb is case insensitive so tables and columns below would clash but sql_ci_no_collision prevents that
    data_1 = {"ItemID": 1, "itemid": "collides"}
    load_info = pipeline.run([data_1], table_name="BigData")

    data_2 = {"1Data": 1, "_1data": "collides"}
    # use colliding table
    load_info = pipeline.run([data_2], table_name="bigdata")

    with pipeline.sql_client() as client:
        from duckdb import DuckDBPyConnection

        conn: DuckDBPyConnection = client.native_connection
        # tags are deterministic so we can just use the naming convention to get table names to select
        first_table = pipeline.default_schema.naming.normalize_table_identifier(
            "BigData"
        )
        sql = f"DESCRIBE TABLE {first_table}"
        print(sql)
        print(conn.sql(sql))
        second_table = pipeline.default_schema.naming.normalize_table_identifier(
            "bigdata"
        )
        sql = f"DESCRIBE TABLE {second_table}"
        print(sql)
        print(conn.sql(sql))

    # print(pipeline.default_schema.to_pretty_yaml())
```

### destination

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/api_reference/dlt/destinations/decorators

Documentation for the dlt.destination function overload that creates a destination factory from a function passed directly as an argument.

```APIDOC
## destination

### Description
Creates a destination factory from a function by directly passing it as an argument. This overload handles direct function calls where the destination function is passed as the first argument, rather than using decorator syntax.

### Method
Function call

### Signature
```python
@overload
def destination(
    func: Callable[Concatenate[Union[TDataItems, str], TTableSchema, TDestinationCallableParams], Any],
    *,
    loader_file_format: TLoaderFileFormat = None,
    batch_size: int = 10,
    name: str = None,
    naming_convention: str = "direct",
    skip_dlt_columns_and_tables: bool = True,
    max_table_nesting: int = 0,
    spec: Type[CustomDestinationClientConfiguration] = None,
    max_parallel_load_jobs: Optional[int] = None,
    loader_parallelism_strategy: Optional[TLoaderParallelismStrategy] = None
) -> Callable[TDestinationCallableParams, _destination]
```

### Parameters
#### Positional Arguments
- **func** (Callable[Concatenate[Union[TDataItems, str], TTableSchema, TDestinationCallableParams], Any]) - Required - A callable that takes two positional arguments "items" and "table", followed by any number of keyword arguments with default values. This function will process the incoming data and does not need to return anything. The keyword arguments can represent configuration or secret values.

#### Keyword Arguments
- **loader_file_format** (TLoaderFileFormat) - Optional - Defines the format in which files are stored in the load package before being sent to the destination function.
- **batch_size** (int) - Optional - Defines how many items per function call are batched together and sent as an array. If set to 0, instead of passing actual data items, you will receive one call per load job with the path of the file as the "items" argument. You can then open and process that file as needed.
- **name** (str) - Optional - Defines the name of the destination created by the destination decorator. Defaults to the name of the function.
- **naming_convention** (str) - Optional - Controls how table and column names are normalized. The default value, "direct", keeps all names unchanged.
- **skip_dlt_columns_and_tables** (bool) - Optional - Defines whether internal dlt tables and columns are included in the custom destination function. Defaults to True.
- **max_table_nesting** (int) - Optional - Defines how deep the normalizer will go to flatten nested fields in your data to create subtables. This overrides any source settings and defaults to 0, meaning no nested tables are created.
- **spec** (Type[CustomDestinationClientConfiguration]) - Optional - Defines a configuration spec used to inject arguments into the decorated function. Arguments not included in the spec will not be injected.
- **max_parallel_load_jobs** (Optional[int]) - Optional - Defines the maximum number of load jobs that can run concurrently during the load process.
- **loader_parallelism_strategy** (Optional[TLoaderParallelismStrategy]) - Optional - Determines the load job parallelism strategy. Can be "sequential" (equivalent to max_parallel_load_jobs=1), "table-sequential" (one load job per table at a time), or "parallel".

### Returns
Callable[TDestinationCallableParams, _destination]: A callable that can be used to create a custom dlt destination instance.

### Example Usage
```python
def my_destination(items, table, api_url: str = dlt.config.value, api_secret = dlt.secrets.value):
    print(table["name"])
    print(items)

dest = dlt.destination(my_destination, batch_size=100, loader_file_format="parquet")
p = dlt.pipeline("chess_pipeline", destination=dest)
```
```

--------------------------------

### Run dlt pipeline to load GitHub data into DuckDB

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/github/load-data-with-python-from-github-to-duckdb

Main pipeline script generated by the dlt CLI at github_pipeline.py. It defines three load functions: one for duckdb issues with full_refresh and limited items, one for airflow events with incremental loading and anonymous access token, and one for all dlthub dlt data. The script runs all three functions when executed directly.

```python
import dlt

from github import github_reactions, github_repo_events


def load_duckdb_repo_reactions_issues_only() -> None:
    """Loads issues, their comments and reactions for duckdb"""
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        "github_reactions",
        destination='duckdb',
        dataset_name="duckdb_issues",
        full_refresh=True,
    )
    # get only 100 items (for issues and pull request)
    data = github_reactions(
        "duckdb", "duckdb", items_per_page=100, max_items=100
    ).with_resources("issues")
    print(pipeline.run(data))


def load_airflow_events() -> None:
    """Loads airflow events. Shows incremental loading. Forces anonymous access token"""
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        "github_events", destination='duckdb', dataset_name="airflow_events"
    )
    data = github_repo_events("apache", "airflow", access_token="")
    print(pipeline.run(data))
    # if you uncomment this, it does not load the same events again
    # data = github_repo_events("apache", "airflow", access_token="")
    # print(pipeline.run(data))


def load_dlthub_dlt_all_data() -> None:
    """Loads all issues, pull requests and comments for dlthub dlt repo"""
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        "github_reactions",
        destination='duckdb',
        dataset_name="dlthub_reactions",
        full_refresh=True,
    )
    data = github_reactions("dlt-hub", "dlt")
    print(pipeline.run(data))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    load_duckdb_repo_reactions_issues_only()
    load_airflow_events()
    load_dlthub_dlt_all_data()
```

### destination(func_or_name, *, loader_file_format, batch_size, name, naming_convention, skip_dlt_columns_and_tables, max_table_nesting, spec, max_parallel_load_jobs, loader_parallelism_strategy, **kwargs)

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/api_reference/dlt/destinations/decorators

Function that can be used as a decorator to create a custom destination or as a function to instantiate a destination.

```APIDOC
## destination(func_or_name: Union[Optional[AnyFun], str] = None, *, loader_file_format: TLoaderFileFormat = None, batch_size: int = 10, name: str = None, naming_convention: str = "direct", skip_dlt_columns_and_tables: bool = True, max_table_nesting: int = 0, spec: Type[CustomDestinationClientConfiguration] = None, max_parallel_load_jobs: Optional[int] = None, loader_parallelism_strategy: Optional[TLoaderParallelismStrategy] = None, **kwargs: Any) -> Any

### Description
When used as a decorator, transforms a function that takes two positional arguments, "items" and "table", along with any number of keyword arguments with default values, into a callable that will create a custom destination. The function itself does not return anything, the keyword arguments can represent configuration or secret values. When used as a function with the first argument being a string (the destination name), instantiates a destination from the provided destination name and type by retrieving the corresponding destination factory and initializing it with the given credentials and keyword arguments.

### Parameters
- **func_or_name** (Union[Optional[AnyFun], str]) - Optional - The function to decorate or the destination name when used as a function.
- **loader_file_format** (TLoaderFileFormat) - Optional - The file format for the loader.
- **batch_size** (int) - Optional - The batch size for loading data. Defaults to 10.
- **name** (str) - Optional - The name of the destination.
- **naming_convention** (str) - Optional - The naming convention for tables. Defaults to "direct".
- **skip_dlt_columns_and_tables** (bool) - Optional - Whether to skip dlt columns and tables. Defaults to True.
- **max_table_nesting** (int) - Optional - The maximum table nesting level. Defaults to 0.
- **spec** (Type[CustomDestinationClientConfiguration]) - Optional - The configuration spec for the destination.
- **max_parallel_load_jobs** (Optional[int]) - Optional - The maximum number of parallel load jobs.
- **loader_parallelism_strategy** (Optional[TLoaderParallelismStrategy]) - Optional - The parallelism strategy for the loader.
- **kwargs** (Any) - Optional - Additional keyword arguments.

### Returns
- **Any** - A callable that creates a custom destination when used as a decorator, or an initialized destination when used as a function.
```

### Python script for loading filesystem data to DuckDB

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/filesystem/load-data-with-python-from-filesystem-to-duckdb

This is the main Python script that defines functions to copy files, stream and merge CSV files, read parquet and JSONL files, read Excel files, and incrementally load CSV files based on modification time. It uses the dlt library and the filesystem source. The script ends with a main block that calls each function in sequence.

```python
import dlt
from dlt.sources.helpers.filesystem import filesystem

# Path to the test bucket - replace with your own bucket URL
TESTS_BUCKET_URL = "s3://dlt-ci-test-bucket"


def copy_files_resource(source_bucket_url: str) -> None:
    """
    Copies files from a source bucket to a local folder using the filesystem resource.
    """
    # Create a pipeline with a unique name and specify the destination
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="standard_filesystem",
        destination='duckdb',
        dataset_name="file_tracker",
    )

    # Use the filesystem resource to list files in the source bucket
    # The file_glob parameter filters files to only those matching the pattern
    # The 'resources' parameter is used to specify the resource name
    # The 'write_disposition' parameter is set to 'replace' to overwrite existing data
    # The 'with_name' method is used to rename the resource
    load_info = pipeline.run(
        filesystem(
            bucket_url=source_bucket_url,
            file_glob="*",
        ).with_name("listing"),
        write_disposition="replace"
    )
    # pretty print the information on data that was loaded
    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)


def stream_and_merge_csv() -> None:
    """
    Streams and merges CSV files from the filesystem into DuckDB.
    """
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="standard_filesystem_csv",
        destination='duckdb',
        dataset_name="file_tracker",
    )

    # Use the filesystem resource to read CSV files
    # The file_glob parameter filters files to only those matching the pattern
    # The 'merge' write disposition is used to merge data based on the primary key
    # The 'with_name' method is used to rename the resource
    load_info = pipeline.run(
        filesystem(
            bucket_url=TESTS_BUCKET_URL,
            file_glob="csv/*",
        ).with_name("csv_files"),
        write_disposition="merge",
        primary_key="id",
    )
    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)


def read_parquet_and_jsonl_chunked() -> None:
    """
    Reads parquet and JSONL files from the filesystem in chunks.
    """
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="standard_filesystem_parquet",
        destination='duckdb',
        dataset_name="file_tracker",
    )

    # Use the filesystem resource to read parquet and JSONL files
    # The file_glob parameter filters files to only those matching the pattern
    # The 'chunk_size' parameter is used to read files in chunks
    load_info = pipeline.run(
        filesystem(
            bucket_url=TESTS_BUCKET_URL,
            file_glob="parquet/*",
            chunk_size=1000,
        ).with_name("parquet_files"),
        write_disposition="replace",
    )
    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)

    load_info = pipeline.run(
        filesystem(
            bucket_url=TESTS_BUCKET_URL,
            file_glob="jsonl/*",
            chunk_size=1000,
        ).with_name("jsonl_files"),
        write_disposition="replace",
    )
    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)


def read_custom_file_type_excel() -> None:
    """
    Reads Excel files from the filesystem using a custom file type.
    """
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="standard_filesystem_excel",
        destination='duckdb',
        dataset_name="file_tracker",
    )

    # Use the filesystem resource to read Excel files
    # The file_glob parameter filters files to only those matching the pattern
    # The 'file_type' parameter is set to 'excel' to read Excel files
    load_info = pipeline.run(
        filesystem(
            bucket_url=TESTS_BUCKET_URL,
            file_glob="excel/*",
            file_type="excel",
        ).with_name("excel_files"),
        write_disposition="replace",
    )
    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)


def read_files_incrementally_mtime() -> None:
    """
    Reads files incrementally based on modification time.
    """
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="standard_filesystem_incremental",
        destination='duckdb',
        dataset_name="file_tracker",
    )

    # here we modify filesystem resource so it will track only new csv files
    # such resource may be then combined with transformer doing further processing
    new_files = filesystem(bucket_url=TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="csv/*")
    # add incremental on modification time
    new_files.apply_hints(incremental=dlt.sources.incremental("modification_date"))
    load_info = pipeline.run((new_files | read_csv()).with_name("csv_files"))
    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)

    # load again - no new files!
    new_files = filesystem(bucket_url=TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="csv/*")
    # add incremental on modification time
    new_files.apply_hints(incremental=dlt.sources.incremental("modification_date"))
    load_info = pipeline.run((new_files | read_csv()).with_name("csv_files"))
    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    copy_files_resource("_storage")
    stream_and_merge_csv()
    read_parquet_and_jsonl_chunked()
    read_custom_file_type_excel()
    read_files_incrementally_mtime()
    read_csv_with_duckdb()
    read_csv_duckdb_compressed()

```

### DestinationReference

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/api_reference/dlt/common/destination/reference

This class provides methods to register, find, and instantiate destination factories, as well as utilities for normalizing and qualifying destination references.

```APIDOC
## DestinationReference Objects

### Description
A registry of destination factories with a set of methods for finding and instantiating destinations.

### Class
`DestinationReference()`

### Attributes
- **DESTINATIONS** - A registry of all the destination factories.

### Methods

#### register

##### Description
Registers a factory class under a reference string.

##### Signature
```python
@classmethod
def register(cls, factory: Type[AnyDestination_CO], ref: str) -> None
```

##### Parameters
- **factory** (Type[AnyDestination_CO]) - Required - The destination factory class to register.
- **ref** (str) - Required - The reference string under which the factory is registered.

#### find

##### Description
Finds or auto-imports a destination factory that can be further called to instantiate it. The ref can be a destination name or import path pointing to a destination class (e.g. `dlt.destinations.postgres`).

##### Signature
```python
@classmethod
def find(
    cls,
    ref: str,
    raise_exec_errors: bool = False,
    import_missing_modules: bool = False
) -> Union[Type[AnyDestination], Callable[..., AnyDestination]]
```

##### Parameters
- **ref** (str) - Required - The destination name or import path.
- **raise_exec_errors** (bool) - Optional - If True, re-raises code execution errors in imported modules.
- **import_missing_modules** (bool) - Optional - If True, ignores missing dependencies during import by substituting them with dummy modules. Should only be used to manipulate local dev environment.

##### Returns
- **Union[Type[AnyDestination], Callable[..., AnyDestination]]** - The destination factory class or a callable that creates a factory instance.

#### ensure_factory

##### Description
Extracts the factory type from a callable that creates a factory instance.

##### Signature
```python
@classmethod
def ensure_factory(
    cls, ref_factory: Union[Type[AnyDestination], Callable[..., AnyDestination]]
) -> Type[AnyDestination]
```

##### Parameters
- **ref_factory** (Union[Type[AnyDestination], Callable[..., AnyDestination]]) - Required - The factory class or callable.

##### Returns
- **Type[AnyDestination]** - The factory type.

#### from_reference

##### Description
Instantiates a destination from a string reference. The ref can be a destination name or import path pointing to a destination class (e.g. `dlt.destinations.postgres`). This method obtains a destination factory and then instantiates it passing the arguments after `ref`.

##### Signature
```python
@classmethod
def from_reference(
    cls,
    ref: str,
    credentials: Optional[Any] = None,
    destination_name: Optional[str] = None,
    environment: Optional[str] = None,
    **kwargs: Any
) -> Optional[AnyDestination]
```

##### Parameters
- **ref** (str) - Required - The destination name or import path.
- **credentials** (Optional[Any]) - Optional - Credentials for the destination.
- **destination_name** (Optional[str]) - Optional - The destination name.
- **environment** (Optional[str]) - Optional - The environment.
- **kwargs** (Any) - Optional - Additional keyword arguments passed to the factory.

##### Returns
- **Optional[AnyDestination]** - The instantiated destination, or None if not found.

#### normalize_type

##### Description
Normalizes a destination type string into a canonical form. Assumes that type names without dots correspond to built-in destinations.

##### Signature
```python
@staticmethod
def normalize_type(destination_type: str) -> str
```

##### Parameters
- **destination_type** (str) - Required - The destination type string.

##### Returns
- **str** - The normalized destination type.

#### to_fully_qualified_refs

##### Description
Converts a ref into fully qualified form, returning one or more alternatives for shorthand notations. Run context is injected if needed. Following formats are recognized:
- name (the last component of destination type serves as destination name if not explicitly specified)

##### Signature
```python
@staticmethod
def to_fully_qualified_refs(ref: str) -> List[str]
```

##### Parameters
- **ref** (str) - Required - The reference string.

##### Returns
- **List[str]** - A list of fully qualified reference alternatives.
```

### Enable atomic replace in BigQuery destination config

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/dlt-ecosystem/destinations/bigquery.md

Enable atomic, metadata-preserving replace for BigQuery by setting enable_atomic_replace to true in the destination configuration. Requires a Google Cloud Storage staging destination; otherwise dlt logs a warning and falls back to regular truncate-and-insert.

[destination.bigquery]
enable_atomic_replace = true

### Generated filesystem_pipeline.py for local filesystem to AlloyDB

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/filesystem-local/load-data-with-python-from-filesystem-local-to-alloydb

Main pipeline script generated by dlt CLI for loading local filesystem data into AlloyDB. Contains functions for streaming and merging CSV files, reading CSV with DuckDB, reading compressed CSV with DuckDB, and reading JSONL/Parquet files in chunks.

```python
import os
import posixpath
from typing import Iterator

import dlt
from dlt.sources import TDataItems

try:
    from .filesystem import FileItemDict, filesystem, readers, read_csv  # type: ignore
except ImportError:
    from filesystem import (
        FileItemDict,
        filesystem,
        readers,
        read_csv,
    )


TESTS_BUCKET_URL = posixpath.abspath("../tests/filesystem/samples/")


def stream_and_merge_csv() -> None:
    """Demonstrates how to scan folder with csv files, load them in chunk and merge on date column with the previous load"""
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="standard_filesystem_csv",
        destination='postgres',
        dataset_name="met_data",
    )
    # met_data contains 3 columns, where "date" column contain a date on which we want to merge
    # load all csvs in A801
    met_files = readers(
        bucket_url=TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="met_csv/A801/*.csv"
    ).read_csv()
    # tell dlt to merge on date
    met_files.apply_hints(write_disposition="merge", merge_key="date")
    # NOTE: we load to met_csv table
    load_info = pipeline.run(met_files.with_name("met_csv"))
    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)

    # now let's simulate loading on next day. not only current data appears but also updated record for the previous day are present
    # all the records for previous day will be replaced with new records
    met_files = readers(
        bucket_url=TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="met_csv/A801/*.csv"
    ).read_csv()
    met_files.apply_hints(write_disposition="merge", merge_key="date")
    load_info = pipeline.run(met_files.with_name("met_csv"))

    # you can also do dlt pipeline standard_filesystem_csv show to confirm that all A801 were replaced with A803 records for overlapping day
    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)


def read_csv_with_duckdb() -> None:
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="standard_filesystem",
        destination='postgres',
        dataset_name="met_data_duckdb",
    )

    # load all the CSV data, excluding headers
    met_files = readers(
        bucket_url=TESTS_BUCKET_URL, file_glob="met_csv/A801/*.csv"
    ).read_csv_duckdb(chunk_size=1000, header=True)

    load_info = pipeline.run(met_files)

    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)


def read_csv_duckdb_compressed() -> None:
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="standard_filesystem",
        destination='postgres',
        dataset_name="taxi_data",
        full_refresh=True,
    )

    met_files = readers(
        bucket_url=TESTS_BUCKET_URL,
        file_glob="gzip/*",
    ).read_csv_duckdb()

    load_info = pipeline.run(met_files)
    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)


def read_parquet_and_jsonl_chunked() -> None:

        dataset_name="teams_data",

### Main pipeline script (slack_pipeline.py)

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/slack/load-data-with-python-from-slack-to-duckdb

The generated pipeline script that loads Slack data into DuckDB. It defines three functions: load_all_resources, select_resource, and get_users, each creating a dlt pipeline and running a Slack source. The script is executed when run as a main module.

```python

"""Pipeline to load slack into duckdb."""

from typing import List

import dlt
from pendulum import datetime
from slack import slack_source


def load_all_resources() -> None:
    """Load all resources from slack without any selection of channels."""

    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="slack", destination='duckdb', dataset_name="slack_data"
    )

    source = slack_source(
        page_size=1000, start_date=datetime(2023, 9, 1), end_date=datetime(2023, 9, 8)
    )

    # Uncomment the following line to load only the access_logs resource. It is not selectes
    # by default because it is a resource just available on paid accounts.
    # source.access_logs.selected = True

    load_info = pipeline.run(
        source,
    )
    print(load_info)


def select_resource(selected_channels: List[str]) -> None:
    """Execute a pipeline that will load the given Slack list of channels with the selected
    channels incrementally beginning at the given start date."""

    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="slack", destination='duckdb', dataset_name="slack_data"
    )

    source = slack_source(
        page_size=20,
        selected_channels=selected_channels,
        start_date=datetime(2023, 9, 1),
        end_date=datetime(2023, 9, 8),
    ).with_resources("channels", "1-announcements", "dlt-github-ci")

    load_info = pipeline.run(
        source,
    )
    print(load_info)


def get_users() -> None:
    """Execute a pipeline that will load Slack users list."""

    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="slack", destination='duckdb', dataset_name="slack_data"
    )

    source = slack_source(
        page_size=20,
    ).with_resources("users")

    load_info = pipeline.run(
        source,
    )
    print(load_info)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Add your desired resources to the list...
    # resources = ["access_logs", "conversations", "conversations_history"]

    # load_all_resources()
    # select_resource(selected_channels=["dlt-github-ci"])

    # select_resource(selected_channels=["1-announcements", "dlt-github-ci"])

    get_users()

```

### Run Jira pipeline with dlt and DuckDB

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/jira/load-data-with-python-from-jira-to-duckdb

Main pipeline script generated by the dlt CLI. Defines two functions: load() loads all Jira resources into a DuckDB dataset named 'jira', and load_query_data() loads issues from JQL queries into a dataset named 'jira_search'. The script runs both functions when executed directly.

```python
from typing import List, Optional

import dlt
from jira import jira, jira_search


def load(endpoints: Optional[List[str]] = None) -> None:
    """
    Load data from specified Jira endpoints into a dataset.

    Args:
        endpoints: A list of Jira endpoints. If not provided, defaults to all resources.
    """
    if not endpoints:
        endpoints = list(jira().resources.keys())

    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="jira_pipeline", destination='duckdb', dataset_name="jira"
    )

    load_info = pipeline.run(jira().with_resources(*endpoints))

    print(f"Load Information: {load_info}")


def load_query_data(queries: List[str]) -> None:
    """
    Load issues from specified Jira queries into a dataset.

    Args:
        queries: A list of JQL queries.
    """
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="jira_search_pipeline",
        destination='duckdb',
        dataset_name="jira_search",
    )

    load_info = pipeline.run(jira_search().issues(jql_queries=queries))

    print(f"Load Information: {load_info}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Add your desired endpoints to the list 'endpoints'
    load(endpoints=None)

    queries = [
        "created >= -30d order by created DESC",
        'project = KAN AND status = "In Progress" order by created DESC',
    ]

    load_query_data(queries=queries)
```

### Run pipeline with sql_table and limit

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/sql_database_hana/load-data-with-python-from-sql_database_hana-to-duckdb

Loads a table from MySQL using sql_table, applies a limit to fetch only one chunk (10 records), and prints normalization info and schema. The example uses the Rfam database and DuckDB destination.

    family = sql_table(
        credentials="mysql+pymysql://rfamro@mysql-rfam-public.ebi.ac.uk:4497/Rfam",
        table="family",
        chunk_size=10,
        detect_precision_hints=True,
        table_adapter_callback=table_adapter,
    )

### Databricks destination with Iceberg and partitioning

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/release-notes/1.18.md

Use the Databricks destination with Iceberg table format, partitioning, and clustering hints. In dlt 1.18 these hints are enforced, and invalid combinations (e.g., mixing partitioning with clustering) are rejected early.

```python
import dlt
from dlt.destinations.adapters import databricks_adapter

pipeline = dlt.pipeline(pipeline_name="to_databricks", destination="databricks")

@dlt.resource
def my_data():
    for i in range(10):
        yield {
            "event_id": i,
            "year": 2024,
            "month": (i % 3) + 1,
            "customer_id": i % 5,
        }

# Enable clustering
databricks_adapter(my_data, cluster="AUTO")

# Enable partitioning
databricks_adapter(my_data, partition=["year", "month"])

# Use Iceberg table format
databricks_adapter(my_data, table_format="ICEBERG")

pipeline.run(my_data)
```

### Pipedrive pipeline script with dlt and DuckDB

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/pipedrive/load-data-with-python-from-pipedrive-to-duckdb

Main pipeline script generated by the dlt CLI. It defines three load functions: load_pipedrive loads all data, load_selected_data uses with_resources to select specific tables, and load_from_start_date incrementally loads activities from a given timestamp. The script runs load_from_start_date by default.

```python
import dlt
from pipedrive import pipedrive_source


def load_pipedrive() -> None:
    """Constructs a pipeline that will load all pipedrive data"""
    # configure the pipeline with your destination details
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="pipedrive", destination='duckdb', dataset_name="pipedrive_data"
    )
    load_info = pipeline.run(pipedrive_source())
    print(load_info)


def load_selected_data() -> None:
    """Shows how to load just selected tables using `with_resources`"""
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="pipedrive", destination='duckdb', dataset_name="pipedrive_data"
    )
    # Use with_resources to select which entities to load
    # Note: `custom_fields_mapping` must be included to translate custom field hashes to corresponding names
    load_info = pipeline.run(
        pipedrive_source().with_resources(
            "products", "deals", "deals_participants", "custom_fields_mapping"
        )
    )
    print(load_info)
    # just to show how to access resources within source
    pipedrive_data = pipedrive_source()
    # print source info
    print(pipedrive_data)
    print()
    # list resource names
    print(pipedrive_data.resources.keys())
    print()
    # print `persons` resource info
    print(pipedrive_data.resources["persons"])
    print()
    # alternatively
    print(pipedrive_data.persons)


def load_from_start_date() -> None:
    """Example to incrementally load activities limited to items updated after a given date"""
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="pipedrive", destination='duckdb', dataset_name="pipedrive_data"
    )

    # First source configure to load everything except activities from the beginning
    source = pipedrive_source()
    source.resources["activities"].selected = False

    # Another source configured to activities starting at the given date (custom_fields_mapping is included to translate custom field hashes to names)
    activities_source = pipedrive_source(
        since_timestamp="2023-03-01 00:00:00Z"
    ).with_resources("activities", "custom_fields_mapping")

    # Run the pipeline with both sources
    load_info = pipeline.run([source, activities_source])
    print(load_info)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # run our main example
    # load_pipedrive()
    # load selected tables and display resource info
    # load_selected_data()
    # load activities updated since given date
    load_from_start_date()

```

### Define and run a Python transformation with @dlt.hub.transformation

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/hub/transformations.md

Defines a transformation that selects the first 5 customers ordered by name, runs it against the same dataset, and prints row counts. The resulting table `copied_customers` is created in the same DuckDB schema with the correct schema.

```python
from typing import Any

@dlt.hub.transformation
def copied_customers(dataset: dlt.Dataset) -> Any:
    customers_table = dataset["customers"]
    yield customers_table.order_by("name").limit(5)

# Same pipeline & same dataset
fruitshop_pipeline.run(copied_customers(fruitshop_pipeline.dataset()))

# show rowcounts again, we now have a new table in the schema and the destination
print(fruitshop_pipeline.dataset().row_counts().df())
```

pipeline.run(events())

### get_destination_clients

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/api_reference/dlt/dataset/utils

Creates destination and/or staging job clients and binds them to the provided schema and dataset names. Configuration in the destination SPEC will be resolved. If multi_dataset_default_schema_name is set, each schema gets its own dataset name as dataset_name__{schema.name}, except the default schema that gets dataset_name.

```APIDOC
## get_destination_clients

### Description
Creates destination and/or staging job clients and binds them to `schema` and dataset names. Configuration in destination SPEC will be resolved.

### Signature
```python
def get_destination_clients(
    schema: Schema,
    destination: AnyDestination = None,
    destination_dataset_name: str = None,
    multi_dataset_default_schema_name: str = None,
    staging: AnyDestination = None,
    staging_dataset_name: str = None
) -> Tuple[JobClientBase, JobClientBase]
```

### Parameters
- **schema** (Schema) - Required - The schema to bind the clients to.
- **destination** (AnyDestination) - Optional - The destination for which to create a job client.
- **destination_dataset_name** (str) - Optional - The dataset name for the destination client.
- **multi_dataset_default_schema_name** (str) - Optional - If set, each schema gets its own dataset name as `dataset_name__{schema.name}`, except the default schema that gets `dataset_name`.
- **staging** (AnyDestination) - Optional - The staging destination for which to create a job client.
- **staging_dataset_name** (str) - Optional - The dataset name for the staging client.

### Returns
- **Tuple[JobClientBase, JobClientBase]** - A tuple containing the destination job client and the staging job client (if staging is provided, otherwise None).
```

### Set ducklake catalog option per_thread_output

Sets the per_thread_output option on the lake_catalog before pipeline runs. Requires a configured pipeline with destination='ducklake' and uses the native duckdb connection from sql_client.

```python
import dlt
import duckdb

pipeline = dlt.pipeline(pipeline_name="foo", destination="ducklake", dataset_name="lake_schema")

# set per thread output option before pipeline runs so options are applied
with pipeline.sql_client() as client:
    con: duckdb.DuckDBPyConnection = client.native_connection
    # set option on `lake_catalog` we configured above
    con.sql("CALL lake_catalog.set_option('per_thread_output', true)")
```

### Define Modal function with dlt pipeline

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/walkthroughs/deploy-a-pipeline/deploy-with-modal.md

Defines a scheduled Modal function that loads tables 'family' and 'genome' from a public MySQL database into DuckDB. Uses minimal reflection to avoid column constraint errors)Skip. In production, store credentials as a Modal Secret.

```py
@app.function(
    volumes={"/data/": vol}, schedule=modal.Period(days=1), serialized=True
)
def load_tables() -> None:
    import dlt
    import os
    from dlt.sources.sql_database import sql_database

    # Define the source database credentials; in production, you would save this as a Modal Secret which can be referenced here as an environment variable
    os.environ[
        "SOURCES__SQL_DATABASE__CREDENTIALS"
    ] = "mysql+pymysql://rfamro@mysql-rfam-public.ebi.ac.uk:4497/Rfam"
    # Load tables "family" and "genome" with minimal reflection to avoid column constraint error
    source = sql_database(reflection_level="minimal").with_resources(
        "family", "genome"
    )

    # Create dlt pipeline object
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="sql_to_duckdb_pipeline",
        destination=dlt.destinations.duckdb(
            "/data/rfam.duckdb"
        ),  # write the duckdb database file to this file location, which will get mounted to the Modal Volume
        dataset_name="sql_to_duckdb_pipeline_data",
        progress="log",  # output progress of the pipeline
    )

    # Run the pipeline
    load_info = pipeline.run(source, write_disposition="replace")

    # Print run statistics
    print(load_info)
```

### Incremental loading with @dlt.resource and dlt.sources.incremental

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/load-data-from-an-api

Use this snippet to load only new issues from the GitHub API by tracking the created_at field. It defines a generator resource that pages through the API, stops when the incremental range is exhausted, and appends new data to DuckDB. Run it twice to see that no duplicate issues are added.

```python
import dlt
from dlt.sources.helpers import requests

@dlt.resource(table_name="issues", write_disposition="append")
def get_issues(
    created_at: dlt.sources.incremental[str] = dlt.sources.incremental(
        "created_at", initial_value="1970-01-01T00:00:00Z"
    ),
) -> Iterator[Dict[str, Any]]:
    # NOTE: we read only open issues to minimize number of calls to the API.
    # There's a limit of ~50 calls for not authenticated Github users.
    url = (
        "https://api.github.com/repos/dlt-hub/dlt/issues"
        "?per_page=100&sort=created&directions=desc&state=open"
    )

    while True:
        response = requests.get(url)
        response.raise_for_status()
        yield response.json()

        # Stop requesting pages if the last element was already
        # older than initial value
        # Note: incremental will skip those items anyway, we just
        # do not want to use the api limits
        if created_at.start_out_of_range:
            break

        # get next page
        if "next" not in response.links:
            break
        url = response.links["next"]["url"]

pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
    pipeline_name="github_issues_incremental",
    destination="duckdb",
    dataset_name="github_data_append",
)

load_info = pipeline.run(get_issues)
row_counts = pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info

print(row_counts)
print("------")
print(load_info)

```

### Incremental loading for filesystem source

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/release-notes/1.17.md

Use incremental loading with the filesystem source to track updated or newly added files. This example sets up a filesystem resource with incremental loading on modification_date and runs a pipeline to DuckDB.

```python
import dlt
from dlt.sources.filesystem import filesystem, read_parquet

filesystem_resource = filesystem(
    bucket_url="s3://my-bucket/files",
    file_glob="**/*.parquet",
    incremental=dlt.sources.incremental("modification_date")
)
pipeline = dlt.pipeline("my_pipeline", destination="duckdb")
pipeline.run((filesystem_resource | read_parquet()).with_name("table_name"))
```

### Enable always_refresh_views for Lance reads

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/dlt-ecosystem/destinations/lance.md

Enable `always_refresh_views` to refresh on every read. This reopens the DuckDB connection and recreates scanner views so reads observe the latest dataset version. Adds a small overhead per read; leave disabled unless you read tables back after writing through a long-lived dataset connection.

```toml
[destination.lance]
always_refresh_views = true
```

### Initialize a new dlt pipeline for IBM Db2 to MotherDuck

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/sql_database_db2/load-data-with-python-from-sql_database_db2-to-motherduck

Create a new directory, initialize a pipeline with the sql_database source and motherduck destination, and install dependencies.

```bash
# create a new directory
mkdir sql_database_db2_pipeline
cd sql_database_db2_pipeline
# initialize a new pipeline with your source and destination
dlt init sql_database motherduck
# install the required dependencies
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

### Fetch data as DataFrame or Arrow table with dlt dataset

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/dlt-ecosystem/transformations/python.md

Reads GitHub reactions from the 'issues' table into a Pandas DataFrame or Arrow table using dlt's dataset access, then computes and prints reaction counts. Requires a dlt pipeline with a DuckDB destination and the dataset access feature.

```python
pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
    pipeline_name="github_pipeline",
    destination="duckdb",
    dataset_name="github_reactions",
    dev_mode=True
)

# get a data frame of all reactions from the dataset
github_issues = pipeline.dataset().table("issues")
reactions = github_issues.select(
    "reactions__+1", "reactions__-1", "reactions__laugh", "reactions__hooray", "reactions__rocket"
).df()

# calculate and print out the sum of all reactions
counts = reactions.sum(0).sort_values(0, ascending=False)
print(counts)

# alternatively, you can fetch the data as an arrow table
reactions = github_issues.select(
    "reactions__+1", "reactions__-1", "reactions__laugh", "reactions__hooray", "reactions__rocket"
).arrow()
# ... do transformations on the arrow table
```

### Run dlt pipeline to load GitHub data into MotherDuck

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/github/load-data-with-python-from-github-to-motherduck

The main pipeline script generated by the dlt CLI at github_pipeline.py. It defines three load functions that use the github source to load data into MotherDuck: duckdb issues (with limited items), airflow events (with incremental loading and anonymous access), and all dlthub dlt data. Run it as a regular Python script after setting up credentials.

```python
import dlt

from github import github_reactions, github_repo_events


def load_duckdb_repo_reactions_issues_only() -> None:
    """Loads issues, their comments and reactions for duckdb"""
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        "github_reactions",
        destination='motherduck',
        dataset_name="duckdb_issues",
        full_refresh=True,
    )
    # get only 100 items (for issues and pull request)
    data = github_reactions(
        "duckdb", "duckdb", items_per_page=100, max_items=100
    ).with_resources("issues")
    print(pipeline.run(data))


def load_airflow_events() -> None:
    """Loads airflow events. Shows incremental loading. Forces anonymous access token"""
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        "github_events", destination='motherduck', dataset_name="airflow_events"
    )
    data = github_repo_events("apache", "airflow", access_token="")
    print(pipeline.run(data))
    # if you uncomment this, it does not load the same events again
    # data = github_repo_events("apache", "airflow", access_token="")
    # print(pipeline.run(data))


def load_dlthub_dlt_all_data() -> None:
    """Loads all issues, pull requests and comments for dlthub dlt repo"""
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        "github_reactions",
        destination='motherduck',
        dataset_name="dlthub_reactions",
        full_refresh=True,
    )
    data = github_reactions("dlt-hub", "dlt")
    print(pipeline.run(data))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    load_duckdb_repo_reactions_issues_only()
    load_airflow_events()
    load_dlthub_dlt_all_data()
```
