### Python script to load data from PostgreSQL to filesystem using dlt

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/sql_database_postgres/load-data-with-python-from-sql_database_postgres-to-filesystem-az

This script defines a dlt pipeline that loads data from a PostgreSQL database to a filesystem destination. It includes functions to load selected tables, with options for backend (connectorx or pandas) and data type handling. The main block runs the load_select_tables_from_database function.

```python
import dlt
from dlt.sources.sql_database import sql_database


def load_select_tables_from_database() -> None:
    """Use the sql_database source to load a few tables from a database."""

    # Load a few tables from the database. The tables are selected by name.
    # The source is configured to use the connectorx backend to read the data.
    # The data is loaded into the 'unsw_flow_7' dataset in the 'speed_test' schema.
    # The chunk_size is set to 100000 rows per batch.
    # The detect_precision_hints option is set to True to keep the source data types.
    # The backend_kwargs option is used to set a separate connection string for connectorx.
    unsw_table = sql_database(
        "postgresql://loader:loader@localhost:5432/dlt_data",
        "unsw_flow_7",
        "speed_test",
        # this is ignored by connectorx
        chunk_size=100000,
        backend="connectorx",
        # keep source data types
        detect_precision_hints=True,
        # just to demonstrate how to setup a separate connection string for connectorx
        backend_kwargs={"conn": "postgresql://loader:loader@localhost:5432/dlt_data"},
    )

    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="unsw_download",
        destination='filesystem',
        # destination=filesystem(os.path.abspath("../_storage/unsw")),
        progress="log",
        full_refresh=True,
    )

    info = pipeline.run(
        unsw_table,
        dataset_name="speed_test",
        table_name="unsw_flow",
        loader_file_format="parquet",
    )
    print(info)


def test_pandas_backend_verbatim_decimals() -> None:
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="rfam_cx",
        destination='filesystem',
        dataset_name="rfam_data_pandas_2",
    )

    def _double_as_decimal_adapter(table: sa.Table) -> None:
        """Emits decimals instead of floats."""
        for column in table.columns.values():
            if isinstance(column.type, sa.Float):
                column.type.asdecimal = True

    sql_alchemy_source = sql_database(
        "mysql+pymysql://rfamro@mysql-rfam-public.ebi.ac.uk:4497/Rfam?&binary_prefix=true",
        backend="pandas",
        table_adapter_callback=_double_as_decimal_adapter,
        chunk_size=100000,
        # set coerce_float to False to represent them as string
        backend_kwargs={"coerce_float": False, "dtype_backend": "numpy_nullable"},
        # preserve full typing info. this will parse
        detect_precision_hints=True,
    ).with_resources("family", "genome")

    info = pipeline.run(sql_alchemy_source)
    print(info)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Load selected tables with different settings

### AdbcArrowLoader subclassing BaseTableLoader

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/dlt-ecosystem/verified-sources/sql_database/advanced.md

Subclasses BaseTableLoader to bypass SQLAlchemy row iteration and read data as Arrow tables via ADBC. Uses compile_query() and get_connection_url() helpers. Requires adbc-driver-manager and adbc-driver-postgresql packages.

```python
from dlt.sources.sql_database import sql_table, BaseTableLoader

class AdbcArrowLoader(BaseTableLoader):
    def load_rows(self, backend_kwargs=None):
        from adbc_driver_manager import dbapi
        from adbc_driver_postgresql import _driver_path
        import pyarrow as pa

        query = self.make_query()
        query_str = self.compile_query(query)
        conn_url = self.get_connection_url()

        with dbapi.connect(driver=_driver_path(), db_kwargs={"uri": conn_url}) as conn:
            with conn.cursor() as cur:
                cur.execute(query_str)
                for batch in cur.fetch_record_batch():
                    yield pa.Table.from_batches([batch], schema=batch.schema)

table = sql_table(
    table="my_table",
    table_loader_class=AdbcArrowLoader,
)
```

### Delete partially-loaded rows for append tables

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/running-in-production/alerting

Manually remove partially-loaded rows for an append table when retrying is not possible. Attach the pipeline, take the load_id of the partially-loaded package, and set root_table to the affected append table. Deletes deepest-first so parent links still resolve.

```python
from dlt.common.schema.utils import get_nested_tables

root_table = "my_table"
schema = pipeline.default_schema

with pipeline.sql_client() as client:

    def load_id_filter(table_name: str) -> str:
        table = schema.tables[table_name]
        load_id_col = client.escape_column_name("_dlt_load_id")
        row_key = client.escape_column_name("_dlt_id")
        parent_key = client.escape_column_name("_dlt_parent_id")
        if table.get("parent") is None:
            return f"{load_id_col} = {client.capabilities.escape_literal(load_id)}"
        parent = client.make_qualified_table_name(table["parent"])
        return (
            f"{parent_key} IN (SELECT {row_key} FROM {parent}"
            f" WHERE {load_id_filter(table['parent'])})"
        )

    # delete the deepest nested tables first so parent links still resolve
    for table in reversed(get_nested_tables(schema.tables, root_table)):
        table_name = client.make_qualified_table_name(table["name"])
        client.execute_sql(
            f"DELETE FROM {table_name} WHERE {load_id_filter(table['name'])}"
        )

```

### Use SQL-like methods on regular relations

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/release-notes/1.13-1.14.md

New SQL-like interface for regular relations in dlt 1.13.0+. Use `dataset.table("customers")` to get a regular relation, then apply sorting with `order_by`, filtering with `filter`, and aggregation with `select` followed by `max().scalar()`. Each method returns results via `.fetchall()` or `.scalar()`.

```python
customers = dataset.table("customers")

# Sort
customers.order_by("created_at").fetchall()

# Filter
customers.filter("id = 1").fetchall()

# Aggregation
customers.select("id").max().scalar()
```

### replication_resource

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/dlt-ecosystem/verified-sources/pg_replication.md

Yields data items for changes in one or more Postgres tables by consuming messages from an existing replication slot and publication.

```APIDOC
## replication_resource

### Description
This resource yields data items for changes in one or more Postgres tables. It consumes messages from an existing replication slot and publication that must be set up beforehand (e.g., using `init_replication`).

### Function Signature
```python
@dlt.resource(
    name=lambda args: args["slot_name"] + "_" + args["pub_name"],
)
def replication_resource(
    slot_name: str,
    pub_name: str,
    credentials: ConnectionStringCredentials = dlt.secrets.value,
    include_columns: Optional[Dict[str, Sequence[str]]] = None,
    columns: Optional[Dict[str, TTableSchemaColumns]] = None,
    target_batch_size: int = 1000,
    flush_slot: bool = True,
) -> Iterable[Union[TDataItem, DataItemWithMeta]]:
    ...
```

### Parameters
- **slot_name** (str) - Required - Name of the replication slot.
- **pub_name** (str) - Required - Name of the publication.
- **credentials** (ConnectionStringCredentials) - Optional - Postgres connection credentials.
- **include_columns** (Optional[Dict[str, Sequence[str]]]) - Optional - Mapping of table names to columns to include.
- **columns** (Optional[Dict[str, TTableSchemaColumns]]) - Optional - Mapping of table names to column schemas.
- **target_batch_size** (int) - Optional - Target batch size for processing (default: 1000).
- **flush_slot** (bool) - Optional - If True, flushes the replication slot after reading (default: True).

### Returns
- **Iterable[Union[TDataItem, DataItemWithMeta]]** - An iterable of data items representing changes.

### Privileges
- REPLICATION attribute (required for logical replication connections)
- Slot ownership (required to consume messages from the replication slot)
- Read access to publication metadata (to query the `pg_publication` system catalog)

### Source Code
For detailed information about the arguments, refer to the [source code](https://github.com/dlt-hub/verified-sources/blob/master/sources/pg_replication/__init__.py).
```

### Load with merge write disposition using apply_hints

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/tutorial/sql-database.md

Loads the 'family' and 'genome' resources with the `merge` write disposition, specifying different primary keys for each table using `apply_hints`. This updates existing data instead of appending or replacing.

```py
import dlt
from dlt.sources.sql_database import sql_database

def load_tables_family_and_genome():

    source = sql_database().with_resources("family", "genome")

    # specify different loading strategy for each resource using apply_hints
    source.family.apply_hints(write_disposition="merge", primary_key="rfam_id") # merge table "family" on column "rfam_id"
    source.genome.apply_hints(write_disposition="merge", primary_key="upid") # merge table "genome" on column "upid"

    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="sql_to_duckdb_pipeline",
        destination="duckdb",
        dataset_name="sql_to_duckdb_pipeline_data"
    )

    load_info = pipeline.run(source)

    print(load_info)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    load_tables_family_and_genome()

```

### range_names

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/dlt-ecosystem/verified-sources/google_sheets.md

The range_names resource processes each range name provided by the source function, loading its data into separate tables in the destination.

```APIDOC
## range_names

### Description
Processes each range name provided by the source function, loading its data into separate tables in the destination.

### Signature
```py
dlt.resource(
     process_range(data, headers=headers, data_types=data_types),
     name=name,
     write_disposition="replace",
)
```

### Parameters
- **process_range** (function) - Required - Function handles rows from a specified Google Spreadsheet range, taking data rows, headers, and data types as arguments.
- **name** (str) - Required - Specifies the table's name, derived from the spreadsheet range.
- **write_disposition** (str) - Required - Dictates how data is loaded to the destination.

### Notes
- Empty rows are ignored.
- Empty cells are converted to None (and then to NULL by dlt).
- Data in columns without headers will be dropped.
```

### clickhouse_adapter

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/api_reference/dlt/destinations/impl/clickhouse/clickhouse_adapter

Adapts data with Clickhouse-specific hints such as table engine type, sort/partition keys, MergeTree settings, and column codecs.

```APIDOC
## clickhouse_adapter

### Description
Adapts the given data by applying Clickhouse-specific hints.

### Signature
```python
def clickhouse_adapter(data: Any,
                       table_engine_type: Optional[TTableEngineType] = None,
                       sort: Optional[TSQLExprOrColumnSeq] = None,
                       partition: Optional[TSQLExprOrColumnSeq] = None,
                       settings: Optional[TMergeTreeSettings] = None,
                       codecs: Optional[TColumnCodecs] = None) -> DltResource
```

### Parameters
- **data** (Any) - Required - The data to be transformed. It can be raw data or an instance of DltResource. If raw data, the function wraps it into a DltResource object.
- **table_engine_type** (TTableEngineType, optional) - Optional - The table index type used when creating the Clickhouse table.
- **sort** (TSQLExprOrColumnSeq, optional) - Optional - Sorting key SQL expression or sequence of column names. Used to generated `ORDER BY` clause of table creation statement. If passing a SQL expression, use normalized column names when referring to columns.
- **partition** (TSQLExprOrColumnSeq, optional) - Optional - Partition key SQL expression or sequence of column names. Used to generated `PARTITION BY` clause of table creation statement. If passing a SQL expression, use normalized column names when referring to columns.
- **settings** (TMergeTreeSettings, optional) - Optional - Dictionary of MergeTree settings to apply to the table. Will be added to `SETTINGS` clause of table creation statement.
- **codecs** (TColumnCodecs, optional) - Optional - Dictionary of codecs to apply to the table's columns. Will be added as `CODEC` clauses in column definitions of table creation statement.

### Returns
- **DltResource** - A resource with applied Clickhouse-specific hints.

### Raises
- **ValueError** - If input for `table_engine_type` is invalid.
- **TypeError** - If input types for `sort`, `partition`, `settings`, or `codecs` are invalid.

### Examples
Set table engine type:
```python
data = [{"name": "Alice", "description": "Software Developer"}]
clickhouse_adapter(data, table_engine_type="merge_tree")
```

Set sort and partition keys:
```python
data = [{"date": "2024-01-01", "town": "Springfield", "street": "Evergreen Terrace"}]
clickhouse_adapter(
    data,
    sort=["town", "street"],  # can also be SQL expression
    partition="toYYYYMM(date)"  # can also be sequence of column names
)
```

Set MergeTree settings:
```python
clickhouse_adapter(
    data,
    settings={"allow_nullable_key": True, "max_suspicious_broken_parts": 500}
)
```

Set column codecs:
```python
clickhouse_adapter(
    data,
    codecs={"town": "LZ4HC", "street": "Delta, ZSTD(2)"}
)
```
```

### Materialize empty schema with explicit columns

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/general-usage/resource.md

Create an empty table by declaring the schema explicitly in the resource decorator and yielding an empty dict. Only metadata columns `_dlt_id` and `_dlt_load_id` will have values. The load fails if any non-metadata column is marked `NOT NULL` (i.e., `"nullable": False`).

```python
@dlt.resource(
    table_name="your_table_name",
    columns={
        "id": {"data_type": "bigint", "nullable": True},
        "event_type": {"data_type": "text", "nullable": True}
    },
    write_disposition="replace"
)
def raw_events():
    yield {}
```

### Load data from SQL database with dlt

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/sql_database_hana/load-data-with-python-from-sql_database_hana-to-cosmosdb

This is the main example from the page, showing how to use the sql_database source to load data from a MySQL database into a Postgres destination. It includes functions for loading select tables with different write dispositions, loading an entire database, using the standalone sql_table resource, and selecting columns. The code is incomplete as the select_columns function is cut off.

```python
from dlt.sources.credentials import ConnectionStringCredentials

from sql_database import sql_database, sql_table, Table


def load_select_tables_from_database() -> None:
    """Use the sql_database source to reflect an entire database schema and load select tables from it.

    This example sources data from the public Rfam MySQL database.
    """
    # Create a pipeline
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="rfam", destination='postgres', dataset_name="rfam_data"
    )

    # Credentials for the sample database.
    # Note: It is recommended to configure credentials in `.dlt/secrets.toml` under `sources.sql_database.credentials`
    credentials = ConnectionStringCredentials(
        "mysql+pymysql://rfamro@mysql-rfam-public.ebi.ac.uk:4497/Rfam"
    )
    # To pass the credentials from `secrets.toml`, comment out the above credentials.
    # And the credentials will be automatically read from `secrets.toml`.

    # Configure the source to load a few select tables incrementally
    source_1 = sql_database(credentials).with_resources("family", "clan")
    # Add incremental config to the resources. "updated" is a timestamp column in these tables that gets used as a cursor
    source_1.family.apply_hints(incremental=dlt.sources.incremental("updated"))
    source_1.clan.apply_hints(incremental=dlt.sources.incremental("updated"))

    # Run the pipeline. The merge write disposition merges existing rows in the destination by primary key
    info = pipeline.run(source_1, write_disposition="merge")
    print(info)

    # Load some other tables with replace write disposition. This overwrites the existing tables in destination
    source_2 = sql_database(credentials).with_resources("features", "author")
    info = pipeline.run(source_2, write_disposition="replace")
    print(info)

    # Load a table incrementally with append write disposition
    # this is good when a table only has new rows inserted, but not updated
    source_3 = sql_database(credentials).with_resources("genome")
    source_3.genome.apply_hints(incremental=dlt.sources.incremental("created"))

    info = pipeline.run(source_3, write_disposition="append")
    print(info)


def load_entire_database() -> None:
    """Use the sql_database source to completely load all tables in a database"""
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="rfam", destination='postgres', dataset_name="rfam_data"
    )

    # By default the sql_database source reflects all tables in the schema
    # The database credentials are sourced from the `.dlt/secrets.toml` configuration
    source = sql_database()

    # Run the pipeline. For a large db this may take a while
    info = pipeline.run(source, write_disposition="replace")
    print(
        humanize.precisedelta(
            pipeline.last_trace.finished_at - pipeline.last_trace.started_at
        )
    )
    print(info)


def load_standalone_table_resource() -> None:
    """Load a few known tables with the standalone sql_table resource, request full schema and deferred
    table reflection"""
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="rfam_database",
        destination='postgres',
        dataset_name="rfam_data",
        full_refresh=True,
    )

    # Load a table incrementally starting at a given date
    # Adding incremental via argument like this makes extraction more efficient
    # as only rows newer than the start date are fetched from the table
    # we also use `detect_precision_hints` to get detailed column schema
    # and defer_table_reflect to reflect schema only during execution
    family = sql_table(
        credentials="mysql+pymysql://rfamro@mysql-rfam-public.ebi.ac.uk:4497/Rfam",
        table="family",
        incremental=dlt.sources.incremental(
            "updated",
        ),
        detect_precision_hints=True,
        defer_table_reflect=True,
    )
    # columns will be empty here due to defer_table_reflect set to True
    print(family.compute_table_schema())

    # Load all data from another table
    genome = sql_table(
        credentials="mysql+pymysql://rfamro@mysql-rfam-public.ebi.ac.uk:4497/Rfam",
        table="genome",
        detect_precision_hints=True,
        defer_table_reflect=True,
    )

    # Run the resources together
    info = pipeline.extract([family, genome], write_disposition="merge")
    print(info)
    # Show inferred columns
    print(pipeline.default_schema.to_pretty_yaml())


def select_columns() -> None:
    """Uses table adapter callback to modify list of columns to be selected"""
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="rfam_database",
        destination='postgres',
        dataset_name="rfam_data_cols",
        full_refresh=True,
    )
```

### Python script to load MySQL data to Snowflake with dlt

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/sql_database_mysql/load-data-with-python-from-sql_database_mysql-to-snowflake

This script defines a dlt pipeline that loads data from a MySQL database to Snowflake. It includes functions to load selected tables, select columns, load the entire database, and use a standalone table resource. The main block runs the load_select_tables_from_database function. The script also includes a test function for pandas backend with verbatim decimals.

```python
import dlt
from dlt.sources.sql_database import sql_database


def load_select_tables_from_database() -> None:
    """Use the sql_database source to load three tables."""

    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="rfam_cx",
        destination='snowflake',
        dataset_name="rfam_data",
    )

    sql_alchemy_source = sql_database(
        "mysql+pymysql://rfamro@mysql-rfam-public.ebi.ac.uk:4497/Rfam?&binary_prefix=true",
        backend="sqlalchemy",
        table_names=["family", "genome", "taxonomy"],
        chunk_size=100000,
        detect_precision_hints=True,
    )

    info = pipeline.run(sql_alchemy_source)
    print(info)


def select_columns() -> None:
    """Load specific columns from a table."""

    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="rfam_cx",
        destination='snowflake',
        dataset_name="rfam_data_columns",
    )

    sql_alchemy_source = sql_database(
        "mysql+pymysql://rfamro@mysql-rfam-public.ebi.ac.uk:4497/Rfam?&binary_prefix=true",
        backend="sqlalchemy",
        table_names=["family"],
        chunk_size=100000,
        detect_precision_hints=True,
    ).with_resources("family")

    # select columns
    sql_alchemy_source.family.apply_hints(
        columns=[
            {"name": "id", "data_type": "bigint", "nullable": False},
            {"name": "short_name", "data_type": "text", "nullable": False},
            {"name": "full_name", "data_type": "text", "nullable": False},
        ]
    )

    info = pipeline.run(sql_alchemy_source)
    print(info)


def load_entire_database() -> None:
    """Use the sql_database source to load all tables from the database."""

    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="rfam_cx",
        destination='snowflake',
        dataset_name="rfam_data_full",
    )

    sql_alchemy_source = sql_database(
        "mysql+pymysql://rfamro@mysql-rfam-public.ebi.ac.uk:4497/Rfam?&binary_prefix=true",
        backend="sqlalchemy",
        chunk_size=100000,
        detect_precision_hints=True,
    )

    info = pipeline.run(sql_alchemy_source)
    print(info)


def select_with_end_value_and_row_order() -> None:
    """Load a table with an end value and row order."""

    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="rfam_cx",
        destination='snowflake',
        dataset_name="rfam_data_incremental",
    )

    sql_alchemy_source = sql_database(
        "mysql+pymysql://rfamro@mysql-rfam-public.ebi.ac.uk:4497/Rfam?&binary_prefix=true",
        backend="sqlalchemy",
        table_names=["family"],
        chunk_size=100000,
        detect_precision_hints=True,
    ).with_resources("family")

    # load up to the row with the max id
    sql_alchemy_source.family.apply_hints(
        incremental=dlt.sources.incremental(
            "id",
            initial_value=1,
            end_value=100000,
            row_order="asc",
        )
    )

    info = pipeline.run(sql_alchemy_source)
    print(info)

    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(

    def _double_as_decimal_adapter(table: sa.Table) -> None:
        """Emits decimals instead of floats."""
        for column in table.columns.values():
            if isinstance(column.type, sa.Float):
                column.type.asdecimal = True

    sql_alchemy_source = sql_database(
        "mysql+pymysql://rfamro@mysql-rfam-public.ebi.ac.uk:4497/Rfam?&binary_prefix=true",
        backend="pandas",
        table_adapter_callback=_double_as_decimal_adapter,
        chunk_size=100000,
        # set coerce_float to False to represent them as string
        backend_kwargs={"coerce_float": False, "dtype_backend": "numpy_nullable"},
        # preserve full typing info. this will parse
        detect_precision_hints=True,
    ).with_resources("family", "genome")

    info = pipeline.run(sql_alchemy_source)
    print(info)

    # as only rows newer than the start date are fetched from the table
    # we also use `detect_precision_hints` to get detailed column schema
    # and defer_table_reflect to reflect schema only during execution
    family = sql_table(
        credentials="mysql+pymysql://rfamro@mysql-rfam-public.ebi.ac.uk:4497/Rfam",
        table="family",
        incremental=dlt.sources.incremental(
            "updated",
        ),
        detect_precision_hints=True,
        defer_table_reflect=True,
    )
    # columns will be empty here due to defer_table_reflect set to True
    print(family.compute_table_schema())

    # Load all data from another table
    genome = sql_table(
        credentials="mysql+pymysql://rfamro@mysql-rfam-public.ebi.ac.uk:4497/Rfam",
        table="genome",
        detect_precision_hints=True,
        defer_table_reflect=True,
    )

    # Run the resources together
    info = pipeline.extract([family, genome], write_disposition="merge")
    print(info)
    # Show inferred columns
    print(pipeline.default_schema.to_pretty_yaml())


def select_columns() -> None:
    """Uses table adapter callback to modify list of columns to be selected"""
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="rfam_database",
        destination='athena',
        dataset_name="rfam_data_cols",
        full_refresh=True,
    )

    def table_adapter(table: Table) -> None:
        print(table.name)
```

### Refresh pipeline with drop_data

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/general-usage/pipeline.md

Use this snippet to truncate tables and reset resource state for selected resources without dropping the tables from the schema. The refresh argument 'drop_data' deletes the data from the tables (e.g., via TRUNCATE) and resets the resource state, which is useful for incremental resources to reload from the initial_value. The schema remains unmodified.

```python
import dlt

pipeline = dlt.pipeline("airtable_demo", destination="duckdb")
pipeline.run(airtable_emojis().with_resources("ðŸ“† Schedule"), refresh="drop_data")
```

### Load MySQL table with ConnectorX and Arrow into DuckDB

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/examples/connector_x_arrow.md

Loads genome data from a public MySQL instance into DuckDB using ConnectorX to produce Arrow tables and dlt to save them as parquet. The resource uses merge write disposition on the `upid` primary key and applies incremental loading on the `created` column. The destination must support parquet files, and running the pipeline again should load no additional records due to incremental loading.

```python
import connectorx as cx

import dlt
from dlt.sources.credentials import ConnectionStringCredentials


def read_sql_x(
    conn_str: ConnectionStringCredentials = dlt.secrets.value,
    query: str = dlt.config.value,
):
    yield cx.read_sql(
        conn_str.to_native_representation(),
        query,
        return_type="arrow",
        protocol="binary",
    )


def genome_resource():
    # create genome resource with merge on `upid` primary key
    genome = dlt.resource(
        name="genome",
        write_disposition="merge",
        primary_key="upid",
    )(read_sql_x)(
        "mysql://rfamro@mysql-rfam-public.ebi.ac.uk:4497/Rfam",  # type: ignore[arg-type]
        "SELECT * FROM genome ORDER BY created LIMIT 1000",
    )
    # add incremental on created at
    genome.apply_hints(incremental=dlt.sources.incremental("created"))
    return genome


if __name__ == "__main__":
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(destination="duckdb")
    genome = genome_resource()

    load_info = pipeline.run(genome)
    print(load_info)
    print(pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info)
    # NOTE: run pipeline again to see that no more records got loaded thanks to incremental loading

    # check that stuff was loaded
    row_counts = pipeline.last_trace.last_normalize_info.row_counts
    assert row_counts["genome"] == 1000
```

### Load data from SQL database to filesystem with dlt

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/sql_database_db2/load-data-with-python-from-sql_database_db2-to-filesystem-aws

This script defines multiple functions to load data from a SQL database to the filesystem destination using dlt. It demonstrates loading select tables with merge and replace write dispositions, loading an entire database, and using the standalone sql_table resource with incremental loading and deferred table reflection. The credentials are provided via a connection string or sourced from secrets.toml.

```python
import sqlalchemy as sa
import humanize

import dlt
from dlt.common import pendulum
from dlt.sources.credentials import ConnectionStringCredentials

from sql_database import sql_database, sql_table, Table


def load_select_tables_from_database() -> None:
    """Use the sql_database source to reflect an entire database schema and load select tables from it.

    This example sources data from the public Rfam MySQL database.
    """
    # Create a pipeline
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="rfam", destination='filesystem', dataset_name="rfam_data"
    )

    # Credentials for the sample database.
    # Note: It is recommended to configure credentials in `.dlt/secrets.toml` under `sources.sql_database.credentials`
    credentials = ConnectionStringCredentials(
        "mysql+pymysql://rfamro@mysql-rfam-public.ebi.ac.uk:4497/Rfam"
    )
    # To pass the credentials from `secrets.toml`, comment out the above credentials.
    # And the credentials will be automatically read from `secrets.toml`.

    # Configure the source to load a few select tables incrementally
    source_1 = sql_database(credentials).with_resources("family", "clan")
    # Add incremental config to the resources. "updated" is a timestamp column in these tables that gets used as a cursor
    source_1.family.apply_hints(incremental=dlt.sources.incremental("updated"))
    source_1.clan.apply_hints(incremental=dlt.sources.incremental("updated"))

    # Run the pipeline. The merge write disposition merges existing rows in the destination by primary key
    info = pipeline.run(source_1, write_disposition="merge")
    print(info)

    # Load some other tables with replace write disposition. This overwrites the existing tables in destination
    source_2 = sql_database(credentials).with_resources("features", "author")
    info = pipeline.run(source_2, write_disposition="replace")
    print(info)

    # Load a table incrementally with append write disposition
    # this is good when a table only has new rows inserted, but not updated
    source_3 = sql_database(credentials).with_resources("genome")
    source_3.genome.apply_hints(incremental=dlt.sources.incremental("created"))

    info = pipeline.run(source_3, write_disposition="append")
    print(info)


def load_entire_database() -> None:
    """Use the sql_database source to completely load all tables in a database"""
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="rfam", destination='filesystem', dataset_name="rfam_data"
    )

    # By default the sql_database source reflects all tables in the schema
    # The database credentials are sourced from the `.dlt/secrets.toml` configuration
    source = sql_database()

    # Run the pipeline. For a large db this may take a while
    info = pipeline.run(source, write_disposition="replace")
    print(
        humanize.precisedelta(
            pipeline.last_trace.finished_at - pipeline.last_trace.started_at
        )
    )
    print(info)


def load_standalone_table_resource() -> None:
    """Load a few known tables with the standalone sql_table resource, request full schema and deferred
    table reflection"""
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="rfam_database",
        destination='filesystem',
        dataset_name="rfam_data",
        full_refresh=True,
    )

    # Load a table incrementally starting at a given date
    # Adding incremental via argument like this makes extraction more efficient
    # as only rows newer than the start date are fetched from the table
    # we also use `detect_precision_hints` to get detailed column schema
    # and defer_table_reflect to reflect schema only during execution
    family = sql_table(
        credentials="mysql+pymysql://rfamro@mysql-rfam-public.ebi.ac.uk:4497/Rfam",
        table="family",
        incremental=dlt.sources.incremental(
            "updated",
        ),
        detect_precision_hints=True,
        defer_table_reflect=True,
    )
    # columns will be empty here due to defer_table_reflect set to True
    print(family.compute_table_schema())

    # Load all data from another table
    genome = sql_table(
        credentials="mysql+pymysql://rfamro@mysql-rfam-public.ebi.ac.uk:4497/Rfam",
        table="genome",
        detect_precision_hints=True,
        defer_table_reflect=True,
    )

    # Run the resources together
    info = pipeline.extract([family, genome], write_disposition="merge")
    print(info)
    # Show inferred columns
    print(pipeline.default_schema.to_pretty_yaml())


def select_columns() -> None:
    """Uses table adapter callback to modify list of columns to be selected"""
```

### Load Airtable tables by name to Athena with column hints

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/airtable/load-data-with-python-from-airtable-to-athena

Loads specific tables from an Airtable base by their names into Athena, applying column hints to silence warnings. Filtering by names is less reliable than by IDs because names can be changed by Airtable users. Uses write_disposition="replace".

```python
def load_select_tables_from_base_by_name(
    base_id: str, table_names: List[str], resources_to_apply_hints: Dict[str, Any]
) -> None:
    """
    Loads specific table names from an Airtable base.

    Args:
        base_id (str): The id of the base. Obtain it, e.g. from the URL in your web browser.
            It starts with "app". See https://support.airtable.com/docs/finding-airtable-ids
        table_names (List[str]): A list of table IDs or table names to load. Unless specified otherwise,
            all tables in the schema are loaded.  Names are freely user-defined. IDs start with "tbl".
            See https://support.airtable.com/docs/finding-airtable-idss
        resources_to_apply_hints (dict): Dict of table names and fields we want to apply hints.

    Note:
        - Filtering by names is less reliable than filtering on IDs because names can be changed by Airtable users.
        - Example in this Airtable URL: https://airtable.com/app7RlqvdoOmJm9XR/tblKHM5s3AujfSbAH
        - Table ID: "tblKHM5s3AujfSbAH"
        - The base_id and table_names can either be passed directly or set up in ".dlt/config.toml".
    """
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="airtable", destination='athena', dataset_name="airtable_data"
    )

    airtables = airtable_source(
        base_id=base_id,
        table_names=table_names,
    )

    # typing columns to silence warnings
    for resource_name, field_names in resources_to_apply_hints.items():
        for field_name in field_names:
            airtables.resources[resource_name].apply_hints(
                columns={field_name: {"name": field_name, "data_type": "text"}}
            )

    load_info = pipeline.run(airtables, write_disposition="replace")
    print(load_info)
```

### Load Chess Data with dlt Pipeline

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/examples/partial_loading.md

Sets up and runs a dlt pipeline to load chess game data from the Chess.com API into a filesystem destination. Generates a list of months, creates a source, runs the pipeline, and then deletes old backfills for each table.

```python
def load_chess_data():
    """
    Sets up and runs the dlt pipeline to load chess game data, then manages backfills.
    """
    # Initialize the dlt pipeline with filesystem destination, here we use local storage
    dest_ = dlt.destinations.filesystem("_storage")
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="chess_com_data", destination=dest_, dataset_name="chess_games"
    )

    # Generate the list of months for the desired date range
    months = list(generate_months(2023, 1, 2023, 12))

    # Create the source with all specified months
    source = chess_com_source("MagnusCarlsen", months)

    # Run the pipeline to fetch and load data
    info = pipeline.run(source)
    print(info)

    # After the run, delete old backfills for each table to maintain data consistency
    for month in months:
        table_name = f"chess_com_games_{month['year']}_{month['month']}"
        delete_old_backfills(info, pipeline, table_name)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    load_chess_data()
```

### Load Airtable tables by ID with dlt

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/airtable/load-data-with-python-from-airtable-to-clickhouse

Loads specific tables from an Airtable base by their IDs into ClickHouse using dlt. The base_id and table_names can be passed directly or set in .dlt/config.toml. Uses write_disposition="replace".

```python
def load_select_tables_from_base_by_id(base_id: str, table_names: List[str]) -> None:
    """
    Load specific table IDs from Airtable to a data pipeline.

    Args:
        base_id (str): The id of the base. Obtain it, e.g. from the URL in your web browser.
            It starts with "app". See https://support.airtable.com/docs/finding-airtable-ids
        table_names (List[str]): A list of table IDs or table names to load. Unless specified otherwise,
            all tables in the schema are loaded.  Names are freely user-defined. IDs start with "tbl".
            See https://support.airtable.com/docs/finding-airtable-ids
        resources_to_apply_hints (dict): Dict of table names and fields we want to apply hints.

    Note:
        - Filtering by names is less reliable than filtering on IDs because names can be changed by Airtable users.
        - Example in this Airtable URL: https://airtable.com/app7RlqvdoOmJm9XR/tblKHM5s3AujfSbAH
        - Table ID: "tblKHM5s3AujfSbAH"
        - The base_id and table_names can either be passed directly or set up in ".dlt/config.toml".
    """

    # configure the pipeline with your destination details
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="airtable", destination='clickhouse', dataset_name="airtable_data"
    )

    airtables = airtable_source(
        base_id=base_id,
        table_names=table_names,
    )

    load_info = pipeline.run(airtables, write_disposition="replace")
    print(load_info)
```

### Python functions for loading data from SQL database with dlt

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/sql_database_hana/load-data-with-python-from-sql_database_hana-to-supabase

This code block defines four functions: load_select_tables_from_database, load_entire_database, load_standalone_table_resource, and select_columns. It demonstrates using the sql_database source to load select tables with incremental and replace write dispositions, loading an entire database, using the standalone sql_table resource with deferred reflection, and selecting columns via a table adapter callback. The code uses credentials from a connection string or from secrets.toml.

```python
from dlt.sources.credentials import ConnectionStringCredentials

from sql_database import sql_database, sql_table, Table


def load_select_tables_from_database() -> None:
    """Use the sql_database source to reflect an entire database schema and load select tables from it.

    This example sources data from the public Rfam MySQL database.
    """
    # Create a pipeline
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="rfam", destination='postgres', dataset_name="rfam_data"
    )

    # Credentials for the sample database.
    # Note: It is recommended to configure credentials in `.dlt/secrets.toml` under `sources.sql_database.credentials`
    credentials = ConnectionStringCredentials(
        "mysql+pymysql://rfamro@mysql-rfam-public.ebi.ac.uk:4497/Rfam"
    )
    # To pass the credentials from `secrets.toml`, comment out the above credentials.
    # And the credentials will be automatically read from `secrets.toml`.

    # Configure the source to load a few select tables incrementally
    source_1 = sql_database(credentials).with_resources("family", "clan")
    # Add incremental config to the resources. "updated" is a timestamp column in these tables that gets used as a cursor
    source_1.family.apply_hints(incremental=dlt.sources.incremental("updated"))
    source_1.clan.apply_hints(incremental=dlt.sources.incremental("updated"))

    # Run the pipeline. The merge write disposition merges existing rows in the destination by primary key
    info = pipeline.run(source_1, write_disposition="merge")
    print(info)

    # Load some other tables with replace write disposition. This overwrites the existing tables in destination
    source_2 = sql_database(credentials).with_resources("features", "author")
    info = pipeline.run(source_2, write_disposition="replace")
    print(info)

    # Load a table incrementally with append write disposition
    # this is good when a table only has new rows inserted, but not updated
    source_3 = sql_database(credentials).with_resources("genome")
    source_3.genome.apply_hints(incremental=dlt.sources.incremental("created"))

    info = pipeline.run(source_3, write_disposition="append")
    print(info)


def load_entire_database() -> None:
    """Use the sql_database source to completely load all tables in a database"""
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="rfam", destination='postgres', dataset_name="rfam_data"
    )

    # By default the sql_database source reflects all tables in the schema
    # The database credentials are sourced from the `.dlt/secrets.toml` configuration
    source = sql_database()

    # Run the pipeline. For a large db this may take a while
    info = pipeline.run(source, write_disposition="replace")
    print(
        humanize.precisedelta(
            pipeline.last_trace.finished_at - pipeline.last_trace.started_at
        )
    )
    print(info)


def load_standalone_table_resource() -> None:
    """Load a few known tables with the standalone sql_table resource, request full schema and deferred
    table reflection"""
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="rfam_database",
        destination='postgres',
        dataset_name="rfam_data",
        full_refresh=True,
    )

    # Load a table incrementally starting at a given date
    # Adding incremental via argument like this makes extraction more efficient
    # as only rows newer than the start date are fetched from the table
    # we also use `detect_precision_hints` to get detailed column schema
    # and defer_table_reflect to reflect schema only during execution
    family = sql_table(
        credentials="mysql+pymysql://rfamro@mysql-rfam-public.ebi.ac.uk:4497/Rfam",
        table="family",
        incremental=dlt.sources.incremental(
            "updated",
        ),
        detect_precision_hints=True,
        defer_table_reflect=True,
    )
    # columns will be empty here due to defer_table_reflect set to True
    print(family.compute_table_schema())

    # Load all data from another table
    genome = sql_table(
        credentials="mysql+pymysql://rfamro@mysql-rfam-public.ebi.ac.uk:4497/Rfam",
        table="genome",
        detect_precision_hints=True,
        defer_table_reflect=True,
    )

    # Run the resources together
    info = pipeline.extract([family, genome], write_disposition="merge")
    print(info)
    # Show inferred columns
    print(pipeline.default_schema.to_pretty_yaml())


def select_columns() -> None:
    """Uses table adapter callback to modify list of columns to be selected"""
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="rfam_database",
        destination='postgres',
        dataset_name="rfam_data_cols",
        full_refresh=True,
    )
```

### evolve_delta_table_schema

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/api_reference/dlt/common/libs/deltalake

Evolves a Delta table schema if different from the given Arrow schema, adding missing columns.

```APIDOC
## evolve_delta_table_schema

### Description
Evolves `delta_table` schema if different from `arrow_schema`. We compare fields via names. Actual types and nullability are ignored. This is how schemas are evolved for other destinations. Existing columns are never modified. Variant columns are created. Adds column(s) to `delta_table` present in `arrow_schema` but not in `delta_table`.

### Signature
```python
def evolve_delta_table_schema(
    delta_table: DeltaTable,
    arrow_schema: pa.Schema
) -> DeltaTable
```

### Parameters
- **delta_table** (DeltaTable) - Required - The Delta table to evolve.
- **arrow_schema** (pa.Schema) - Required - The Arrow schema to evolve to.

### Returns
- **DeltaTable** - The evolved Delta table.
```

### Apply hints and run pipeline with table name

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/general-usage/filesystem

Applies hints to the filesystem pipe to merge on the "date" key and loads data into a table named "table_name". The pipeline uses the "duckdb" destination.

```python
import dlt
from dlt.sources.filesystem import filesystem, read_csv

filesystem_pipe = filesystem(bucket_url="file://Users/admin/Documents/csv_files", file_glob="*.csv") | read_csv()
# Tell dlt to merge on date
filesystem_pipe.apply_hints(write_disposition="merge", merge_key="date")

# We load the data into the table_name table
pipeline = dlt.pipeline(pipeline_name="my_pipeline", destination="duckdb")
load_info = pipeline.run(filesystem_pipe.with_name("table_name"))
print(load_info)

```

### Delta Lake table properties with databricks_adapter

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/dlt-ecosystem/destinations/databricks.md

Configures Delta Lake table properties for performance tuning and metadata. Includes append-only, log retention, data skipping, auto-optimize, and custom properties. Uses cluster="event_date" for clustering.

```python
import dlt
from dlt.destinations.adapters import databricks_adapter

@dlt.resource
def high_volume_events():
    yield from generate_events()  # Your event generator

databricks_adapter(
    high_volume_events,
    table_properties={
        # Delta Lake optimization properties
        "delta.appendOnly": True,  # Table is append-only
        "delta.logRetentionDuration": "30 days",  # Keep logs for 30 days
        "delta.dataSkippingStatsColumns": "event_date,user_id,event_type",  # Columns for data skipping
        "delta.autoOptimize.optimizeWrite": True,  # Enable optimize write
        "delta.autoOptimize.autoCompact": True,  # Enable auto compaction

        # Custom properties for metadata
        "custom.team": "data-engineering",
        "custom.sla": "tier-1",
        "custom.refresh_frequency": "hourly"
    },
    cluster="event_date",
    table_comment="High-volume event stream with Delta optimizations"
)
```

### Join two datasets in-warehouse with dlt.hub.transformation

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/hub/transformations.md

Pass two input datasets to a transformation to join them across datasets. When the output engine can read and write the inputs, the join runs in-warehouse as a model job; otherwise dlt uses eager materialization. Here `crm` and `sales` are in the same DuckDB, so the join runs in-warehouse.

```python
# pass two input datasets. the transformation joins across them
@dlt.hub.transformation(table_name="user_orders")
def user_orders(crm: dlt.Dataset, sales: dlt.Dataset) -> Any:
    yield crm["users"].join(sales["orders"], on="users.id = orders.user_id")

# crm, sales and the marts output all live in the same duckdb, so the join
# runs in-warehouse as a model job â€” no data leaves the destination
marts_pipeline.run(user_orders(crm_pipeline.dataset(), sales_pipeline.dataset()))
```

### Define GitHub REST API configuration and load data into MotherDuck

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/rest_api/load-data-with-python-from-rest_api-to-motherduck

Configures a RESTAPIConfig for the GitHub API with bearer token authentication, incremental loading for issues, and a child resource for issue comments. Then defines a dlt pipeline to load the data into MotherDuck.

```python
# Create a REST API configuration for the GitHub API
# Use RESTAPIConfig to get autocompletion and type checking
config: RESTAPIConfig = {
    "client": {
        "base_url": "https://api.github.com/repos/dlt-hub/dlt/",
        "auth": {
            "type": "bearer",
            "token": github_token,
        },
    },
    # The default configuration for all resources and their endpoints
    "resource_defaults": {
        "primary_key": "id",
        "write_disposition": "merge",
        "endpoint": {
            "params": {
                "per_page": 100,
            },
        },
    },
    "resources": [
        # This is a simple resource definition,
        # that uses the endpoint path as a resource name:
        # "pulls",
        # Alternatively, you can define the endpoint as a dictionary
        # {
        #     "name": "pulls", # <- Name of the resource
        #     "endpoint": "pulls",  # <- This is the endpoint path
        # }
        # Or use a more detailed configuration:
        {
            "name": "issues",
            "endpoint": {
                "path": "issues",
                # Query parameters for the endpoint
                "params": {
                    "sort": "updated",
                    "direction": "desc",
                    "state": "open",
                    # Define `since` as a special parameter
                    # to incrementally load data from the API.
                    # This works by getting the updated_at value
                    # from the previous response data and using this value
                    # for the `since` query parameter in the next request.
                    "since": {
                        "type": "incremental",
                        "cursor_path": "updated_at",
                        "initial_value": "2024-01-25T11:21:28Z",
                    },
                },
            },
        },
        # The following is an example of a resource that uses
        # a parent resource (`issues`) to get the `issue_number`
        # and include it in the endpoint path:
        {
            "name": "issue_comments",
            "endpoint": {
                # The placeholder {issue_number} will be resolved
                # from the parent resource
                "path": "issues/{issue_number}/comments",
                "params": {
                    # The value of `issue_number` will be taken
                    # from the `number` field in the `issues` resource
                    "issue_number": {
                        "type": "resolve",
                        "resource": "issues",
                        "field": "number",
                    }
                },
            },
            # Include data from `id` field of the parent resource
            # in the child data. The field name in the child data
            # will be called `_issues_id` (_{resource_name}_{field_name})
            "include_from_parent": ["id"],
        },
    ],
}

yield from rest_api_resources(config)


def load_github() -> None:
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="rest_api_github",
        destination='motherduck',
        dataset_name="rest_api_data",
    )

    load_info = pipeline.run(github_source())
    print(load_info)
```

### Load Google Sheets to MSSQL with dlt pipeline functions

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/google_sheets/load-data-with-python-from-google_sheets-to-mssql

Defines five dlt pipeline functions that load Google Sheets data into MSSQL using the google_spreadsheet source. Each function configures a pipeline with destination='mssql' and full_refresh=True, and varies the get_sheets and get_named_ranges flags to load ranges, sheets, named ranges, or combinations. The final function demonstrates loading two spreadsheets in one pipeline and renaming tables via apply_hints, then asserts the resulting table names.

```python
from typing import Sequence

import dlt

from google_sheets import google_spreadsheet


def load_pipeline_with_ranges(
    spreadsheet_url_or_id: str, range_names: Sequence[str]
) -> None:
    """
    Loads explicitly passed ranges
    """
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="google_sheets_pipeline",
        destination='mssql',
        full_refresh=True,
        dataset_name="test",
    )
    data = google_spreadsheet(
        spreadsheet_url_or_id=spreadsheet_url_or_id,
        range_names=range_names,
        get_sheets=False,
        get_named_ranges=False,
    )
    info = pipeline.run(data)
    print(info)


def load_pipeline_with_sheets(spreadsheet_url_or_id: str) -> None:
    """
    Will load all the sheets in the spreadsheet, but it will not load any of the named ranges in the spreadsheet.
    """
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="google_sheets_pipeline",
        destination='mssql',
        full_refresh=True,
        dataset_name="sample_google_sheet_data",
    )
    data = google_spreadsheet(
        spreadsheet_url_or_id=spreadsheet_url_or_id,
        get_sheets=True,
        get_named_ranges=False,
    )
    info = pipeline.run(data)
    print(info)


def load_pipeline_with_named_ranges(spreadsheet_url_or_id: str) -> None:
    """
    Will not load the sheets in the spreadsheet, but it will load all the named ranges in the spreadsheet.
    """
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="google_sheets_pipeline",
        destination='mssql',
        full_refresh=True,
        dataset_name="sample_google_sheet_data",
    )
    data = google_spreadsheet(
        spreadsheet_url_or_id=spreadsheet_url_or_id,
        get_sheets=False,
        get_named_ranges=True,
    )
    info = pipeline.run(data)
    print(info)


def load_pipeline_with_sheets_and_ranges(spreadsheet_url_or_id: str) -> None:
    """
    Will load all the sheets in the spreadsheet and all the named ranges in the spreadsheet.
    """
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="google_sheets_pipeline",
        destination='mssql',
        full_refresh=True,
        dataset_name="sample_google_sheet_data",
    )
    data = google_spreadsheet(
        spreadsheet_url_or_id=spreadsheet_url_or_id,
        get_sheets=True,
        get_named_ranges=True,
    )
    info = pipeline.run(data)
    print(info)


def load_with_table_rename_and_multiple_spreadsheets(
    spreadsheet_url_or_id: str, range_names: Sequence[str]
) -> None:
    """Demonstrates how to load two spreadsheets in one pipeline and how to rename tables"""

    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="google_sheets_pipeline",
        destination='mssql',
        full_refresh=True,
        dataset_name="sample_google_sheet_data",
    )

    # take data from spreadsheet 1
    data = google_spreadsheet(
        spreadsheet_url_or_id=spreadsheet_url_or_id,
        range_names=[range_names[0]],
        get_named_ranges=False,
    )

    # take data from spreadsheet 2
    data_2 = google_spreadsheet(
        spreadsheet_url_or_id=spreadsheet_url_or_id,
        range_names=[range_names[1]],
        get_named_ranges=False,
    )
    # apply the table name to the existing resource: the resource name is the name of the range
    data.resources[range_names[0]].apply_hints(table_name="first_sheet_data")
    data_2.resources[range_names[1]].apply_hints(table_name="second_sheet_data")

    # load two spreadsheets
    info = pipeline.run([data, data_2])
    print(info)
    # yes the tables are there
    user_tables = pipeline.default_schema.data_tables()
    # check if table is there
    assert {t["name"] for t in user_tables} == {
        "first_sheet_data",
        "second_sheet_data",
        "spreadsheet_info",
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    url_or_id = "1HhWHjqouQnnCIZAFa2rL6vT91YRN8aIhts22SUUR580"
    range_names = ["hidden_columns_merged_cells", "Blank Columns"]

    load_pipeline_with_ranges(url_or_id, range_names)
    load_pipeline_with_sheets(url_or_id)
    load_pipeline_with_named_ranges(url_or_id)
    load_pipeline_with_sheets_and_ranges(url_or_id)
    load_with_table_rename_and_multiple_spreadsheets(url_or_id, range_names)
```

### Load standalone table resources with sql_table

Loads specific tables using the standalone sql_table resource with incremental loading, precision hints, and deferred table reflection. Shows how to extract multiple resources together and print inferred schema.

    # and defer_table_reflect to reflect schema only during execution

        table="family",

            "updated",
        ),
        detect_precision_hints=True,
        defer_table_reflect=True,
    )

    print(family.compute_table_schema())

    genome = sql_table(
        credentials="mysql+pymysql://rfamro@mysql-rfam-public.ebi.ac.uk:4497/Rfam",
        table="genome",
        detect_precision_hints=True,
        defer_table_reflect=True,
    )

    # Run the resources together
    info = pipeline.extract([family, genome], write_disposition="merge")
    print(info)
    # Show inferred columns
    print(pipeline.default_schema.to_pretty_yaml())

### Select columns with table adapter

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/sql_database_mysql/load-data-with-python-from-sql_database_mysql-to-duckdb

Defines a function that uses a table adapter callback to modify the list of columns to be selected from a MySQL table. It demonstrates how to remove a column from the SqlAlchemy table object and load the table with a merge write disposition.

```python
def select_columns() -> None:
    """Uses table adapter callback to modify list of columns to be selected"""
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="rfam_database",
        destination='duckdb',
        dataset_name="rfam_data_cols",
        full_refresh=True,
    )

    def table_adapter(table: Table) -> None:
        print(table.name)
        if table.name == "family":
            # this is SqlAlchemy table. _columns are writable
            # let's drop updated column
            table._columns.remove(table.columns["updated"])

    family = sql_table(
        credentials="mysql+pymysql://rfamro@mysql-rfam-public.ebi.ac.uk:4497/Rfam",
        table="family",
        table_adapter_callback=table_adapter,
    )
```

### Load standalone table resources into Databricks

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/sql_database_db2/load-data-with-python-from-sql_database_db2-to-databricks

Defines a function that uses the standalone sql_table resource to load specific tables (family, genome) from the Rfam database into Databricks. It demonstrates incremental loading, detect_precision_hints, and defer_table_reflect. Prints the computed table schema and the pipeline default schema.

```python
def load_standalone_table_resource() -> None:

    table reflection"""

        pipeline_name="rfam_database",

        detect_precision_hints=True,

### Define the metrics_table transformer

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/dlt-ecosystem/verified-sources/google_analytics.md

This transformer extracts data from metadata and populates a table called 'metrics' with each metric. It uses a write disposition of 'replace'.

```py
@dlt.transformer(data_from=get_metadata, write_disposition="replace", name="metrics")
def metrics_table(metadata: Metadata) -> Iterator[TDataItem]:
    for metric in metadata.metrics:
        yield to_dict(metric)
```

### Migrate to Ibis table relations with table_type="ibis"

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/release-notes/1.13-1.14.md

Required migration for accessing Ibis table relations in dlt 1.12.3+. Previously, `dataset["customers"]` returned an Ibis relation; now it returns a regular relation. To get an Ibis table relation, explicitly set `table_type="ibis"` to get the table expression first, then convert it to a table relation using `dataset(customers_expression)`. The resulting relation can be fetched as a DataFrame with `.df()`.

```python
# Previously: dataset["customers"]  # now returns a regular relation
customers_expression = dataset.table("customers", table_type="ibis")
customers_relation = dataset(customers_expression)

df = customers_relation.df()  # fetch as DataFrame
```

### Load select tables from database with incremental and replace write dispositions

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/sql_database_oracle/load-data-with-python-from-sql_database_oracle-to-postgres

Defines a function that uses the sql_database source to reflect an entire database schema and load select tables. It demonstrates incremental loading with the 'updated' column as a cursor, merge write disposition, replace write disposition for other tables, and append write disposition for a table with only new rows.

```python
from dlt.sources.credentials import ConnectionStringCredentials

from sql_database import sql_database, sql_table, Table


def load_select_tables_from_database() -> None:
    """Use the sql_database source to reflect an entire database schema and load select tables from it.

    This example sources data from the public Rfam MySQL database.
    """
    # Create a pipeline
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="rfam", destination='postgres', dataset_name="rfam_data"
    )

    # Credentials for the sample database.
    # Note: It is recommended to configure credentials in `.dlt/secrets.toml` under `sources.sql_database.credentials`
    credentials = ConnectionStringCredentials(
        "mysql+pymysql://rfamro@mysql-rfam-public.ebi.ac.uk:4497/Rfam"
    )
    # To pass the credentials from `secrets.toml`, comment out the above credentials.
    # And the credentials will be automatically read from `secrets.toml`.

    # Configure the source to load a few select tables incrementally
    source_1 = sql_database(credentials).with_resources("family", "clan")
    # Add incremental config to the resources. "updated" is a timestamp column in these tables that gets used as a cursor
    source_1.family.apply_hints(incremental=dlt.sources.incremental("updated"))
    source_1.clan.apply_hints(incremental=dlt.sources.incremental("updated"))

    # Run the pipeline. The merge write disposition merges existing rows in the destination by primary key
    info = pipeline.run(source_1, write_disposition="merge")
    print(info)

    # Load some other tables with replace write disposition. This overwrites the existing tables in destination
    source_2 = sql_database(credentials).with_resources("features", "author")
    info = pipeline.run(source_2, write_disposition="replace")
    print(info)

    # Load a table incrementally with append write disposition
    # this is good when a table only has new rows inserted, but not updated
    source_3 = sql_database(credentials).with_resources("genome")
    source_3.genome.apply_hints(incremental=dlt.sources.incremental("created"))

    info = pipeline.run(source_3, write_disposition="append")
    print(info)
```

### Send Slack notifications for schema updates with dlt

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/general-usage/schema-evolution.md

Iterates over load_info packages and their schema_update tables to send Slack notifications for each column change, including the table name, column name, and data type. Requires a Slack webhook URL and the dlt library.

```python
# Import the send_slack_message function from the dlt library
from dlt.common.runtime.slack import send_slack_message

# Define the URL for your Slack webhook
hook = "https://hooks.slack.com/services/xxx/xxx/xxx"

# Iterate over each package in the load_info object
for package in load_info.load_packages:
    # Iterate over each table in the schema_update of the current package
    for table_name, table in package.schema_update.items():
        # Iterate over each column in the current table
        for column_name, column in table["columns"].items():
            # Send a message to the Slack channel with the table
						# and column update information
            send_slack_message(
                hook,
                message=(
                    f"\tTable updated: {table_name}: "
                    f"Column changed: {column_name}: "
                    f"{column['data_type']}"
                )
            )
```

### Cross-dataset join with two pipelines sharing a DuckDB file

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/general-usage/dataset-access/dataset.md

Sets up two dlt pipelines writing to the same DuckDB file under different dataset names, then joins a Relation from one dataset with a Relation from the other using an explicit `on` condition. Both datasets must share the same data location; cross-dataset joins require `on` and are rejected when relations live in different data locations.

```python
# two pipelines that write to the same DuckDB file under different
# dataset names â€” both datasets share one data location.
db_path = str(tmp_path / "shop.duckdb")

crm_pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
    pipeline_name="crm",
    destination=dlt.destinations.duckdb(db_path),
    dataset_name="crm_data",
)
crm_pipeline.run(
    [{"id": 1, "name": "Alice"}, {"id": 2, "name": "Bob"}],
    table_name="users",
)

sales_pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
    pipeline_name="sales",
    destination=dlt.destinations.duckdb(db_path),
    dataset_name="sales_data",
)
sales_pipeline.run(
    [
        {"id": 10, "user_id": 1, "sku": "W-001", "quantity": 2},
        {"id": 11, "user_id": 1, "sku": "G-001", "quantity": 1},
        {"id": 12, "user_id": 2, "sku": "W-001", "quantity": 1},
    ],
    table_name="purchases",
)

crm = crm_pipeline.dataset()
sales = sales_pipeline.dataset()

# pass the right-hand side as a Relation from the other dataset.
# cross-dataset joins require `on`.
users_with_purchases = crm["users"].join(
    sales["purchases"],
    on="users.id = purchases.user_id",
)
df = users_with_purchases.df()
```

def test_pandas_backend_verbatim_decimals() -> None:
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="rfam_cx",

        dataset_name="rfam_data_pandas_2",
    )

    def _double_as_decimal_adapter(table: sa.Table) -> None:
        """Emits decimals instead of floats."""
        for column in table.columns.values():
            if isinstance(column.type, sa.Float):
                column.type.asdecimal = True

    sql_alchemy_source = sql_database(

        backend_kwargs={"coerce_float": False, "dtype_backend": "numpy_nullable"},
        # preserve full typing info. this will parse
        detect_precision_hints=True,

### Normalized SQL query with dlt columns

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/hub/transformations.md

The normalized query after the extract stage. It adds the `_dlt_load_id` and `_dlt_id` columns and wraps the original query in a subquery.

```sql
SELECT
    _dlt_subquery."id" AS "id",
    _dlt_subquery."value" AS "value",
    '1749134128.17655' AS "_dlt_load_id",
    UUID() AS "_dlt_id"
FROM (
    SELECT
        "my_table"."id" AS "id",
        "my_table"."value" AS "value"
    FROM "my_pipeline_dataset"."my_table" AS "my_table"
    )
AS _dlt_subquery
```

### Load tables family and genome with sql_database source

```python
import dlt
from dlt.sources.sql_database import sql_database

def load_tables_family_and_genome():

    # Create a dlt source that will load tables "family" and "genome"
    source = sql_database().with_resources("family", "genome")

    # Create a dlt pipeline object
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="sql_to_duckdb_pipeline", # Custom name for the pipeline
        destination="duckdb", # dlt destination to which the data will be loaded
        dataset_name="sql_to_duckdb_pipeline_data" # Custom name for the dataset created in the destination
    )

    # Run the pipeline
    load_info = pipeline.run(source)

    # Pretty print load information
    print(load_info)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    load_tables_family_and_genome()

### Load all tables from Airtable base with column hints

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/airtable/load-data-with-python-from-airtable-to-neondb

Defines a function to load all tables from an Airtable base while applying column hints to silence warnings. It iterates over resources and fields, applying hints with data_type 'text'.

```python
def load_all_tables_from_base_with_hints(base_id: str, resources_to_apply_hints: Dict[str, Any]) -> None:
    """
    Load all tables from an Airtable base and apply hints to columns.

    Args:
        base_id (str): The id of the base. Obtain it, e.g. from the URL in your web browser.
            It starts with "app". See https://support.airtable.com/docs/finding-airtable-ids
        resources_to_apply_hints (dict): Dict of table names and fields we want to apply hints.
    """

    # configure the pipeline with your destination details
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="airtable", destination='postgres', dataset_name="airtable_data"
    )

    airtables = airtable_source(
        base_id=base_id,
    )

    # typing columns to silence warnings
    for resource_name, field_names in resources_to_apply_hints.items():
        for field_name in field_names:
            airtables.resources[resource_name].apply_hints(
                columns={field_name: {"name": field_name, "data_type": "text"}}
            )

    load_info = pipeline.run(airtables, write_disposition="replace")
    print(load_info)
```

### Load Airtable tables by name with column hints

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/airtable/load-data-with-python-from-airtable-to-postgres

Defines a function to load specific tables by name and applies column hints to silence warnings. Uses apply_hints to set data_type to text for specified fields.

```python
def load_select_tables_from_base_by_name(
    base_id: str, table_names: List[str], resources_to_apply_hints: Dict[str, Any]
) -> None:
    """
    Loads specific table names from an Airtable base.

    Args:
        base_id (str): The id of the base. Obtain it, e.g. from the URL in your web browser.
            It starts with "app". See https://support.airtable.com/docs/finding-airtable-ids
        table_names (List[str]): A list of table IDs or table names to load. Unless specified otherwise,
            all tables in the schema are loaded.  Names are freely user-defined. IDs start with "tbl".
            See https://support.airtable.com/docs/finding-airtable-idss
        resources_to_apply_hints (dict): Dict of table names and fields we want to apply hints.

    Note:
        - Filtering by names is less reliable than filtering on IDs because names can be changed by Airtable users.
        - Example in this Airtable URL: https://airtable.com/app7RlqvdoOmJm9XR/tblKHM5s3AujfSbAH
        - Table ID: "tblKHM5s3AujfSbAH"
        - The base_id and table_names can either be passed directly or set up in ".dlt/config.toml".
    """
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="airtable", destination='postgres', dataset_name="airtable_data"
    )

    airtables = airtable_source(
        base_id=base_id,
        table_names=table_names,
    )

    # typing columns to silence warnings
    for resource_name, field_names in resources_to_apply_hints.items():
        for field_name in field_names:
            airtables.resources[resource_name].apply_hints(
                columns={field_name: {"name": field_name, "data_type": "text"}}
            )

    load_info = pipeline.run(airtables, write_disposition="replace")
    print(load_info)
```

### Load stage INSERT statement

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/hub/transformations.md

The final SQL executed during the load stage. It inserts the transformed data into the destination table, materializing the transformation result.

```sql
INSERT INTO
    "my_pipeline_dataset"."my_transformation" ("id", "value", "_dlt_load_id", "_dlt_id")
SELECT
    _dlt_subquery."id" AS "id",
    _dlt_subquery."value" AS "value",
    '1749134128.17655' AS "_dlt_load_id",
    UUID() AS "_dlt_id"
FROM (
    SELECT
        "my_table"."id" AS "id",
        "my_table"."value" AS "value"
    FROM "my_pipeline_dataset"."my_table" AS "my_table"
    )
AS _dlt_subquery
```

### Load incremental ID table with dlt

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/walkthroughs/sql-incremental-configuration.md

Loads the 'contact' table incrementally using the 'id' column as the incremental key. Uses write_disposition='append' to add new records without affecting existing ones.

```python
def load_incremental_id_table_resource() -> None:
    """Load a table incrementally based on an ID."""
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="mysql_database",
        destination='bigquery',
        dataset_name="dlt_contacts",
    )

    # Load table "contact" incrementally based on ID
    source = sql_database().with_resources("contact")
    source.contact.apply_hints(incremental=dlt.sources.incremental("id"))

    # Run the pipeline with append write disposition
    info = pipeline.run(source, write_disposition="append")

    # Print the info
    print(info)
```

### update_dict_nested

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/api_reference/dlt/common/utils

Merges `src` into `dst` key wise. Does not recur into lists. Values in `src` overwrite `dst` if both keys exit. Only `dict` and its subclasses are updated recursively.

```APIDOC
## update_dict_nested

### Description
Merges `src` into `dst` key wise. Does not recur into lists. Values in `src` overwrite `dst` if both keys exit. Only `dict` and its subclasses are updated recursively. With `copy_src_dicts`, dict key:values will be deep copied, otherwise, both dst and src will keep the same references.

### Method
Function

### Endpoint
`update_dict_nested(dst: TDict, src: TDict, copy_src_dicts: bool = False) -> TDict`

### Parameters
- **dst** (TDict) - Required - Destination dictionary to merge into.
- **src** (TDict) - Required - Source dictionary to merge from.
- **copy_src_dicts** (bool) - Optional - If `True`, dict values in `src` are deep copied; otherwise, references are shared. Default is `False`.

### Returns
- **TDict** - The merged dictionary.

```

### retrieve_a_hosted_page

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/pipelines/chargebee/load-data-with-python-from-chargebee-to-supabase

Configures the Chargebee source to retrieve a hosted page by its ID. The endpoint is /hosted_pages/{hosted-page-id} and the data is stored in the hosted_page table with a merge write disposition.

```APIDOC
## GET /hosted_pages/{hosted-page-id}

### Description
Retrieves a hosted page from Chargebee. The response content varies based on the type of hosted page, including customer, subscription, card, invoice, transactions, or retention details.

### Method
GET

### Endpoint
/hosted_pages/{hosted-page-id}

### Parameters
#### Path Parameters
- **hosted-page-id** (string) - Required - The unique identifier of the hosted page to retrieve.

### Request Example
No request body required.

### Response
#### Success Response (200)
- **hosted_page** (object) - The hosted page object containing the following fields based on the type:
  - **type** (string) - The type of hosted page (e.g., checkout_new, checkout_existing, update_payment_method, pre_cancel, collect_now).
  - **content** (object) - The content of the hosted page, which varies by type:
    - For `checkout_new` and `checkout_existing`: includes `customer`, `subscription`, `card`, and `invoice` objects.
    - For `update_payment_method`: includes `customer` and `card` objects.
    - For `pre_cancel`: includes `retention` object with a `bypass` flag.
    - For `collect_now`: includes `transactions` list and `customer` object.

#### Response Example
{
  "hosted_page": {
    "id": "hp_123",
    "type": "checkout_new",
    "content": {
      "customer": { "id": "cus_123", "email": "customer@example.com" },
      "subscription": { "id": "sub_123", "status": "active" },
      "card": { "id": "card_123", "last4": "4242" },
      "invoice": { "id": "inv_123", "total": 100 }
    }
  }
}
```

### Filter relation with dlt.sources.incremental cursor

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/general-usage/dataset-access/dataset.md

Use Relation.incremental() to filter a relation to rows in the cursor window. The first block shows the bounded read with a cursor on the 'created_at' column; the second shows passing the same cursor directly to dataset.table().

```py
import dlt
from dlt.common.pendulum import pendulum

dataset = pipeline.dataset()

# bounded read: all rows in [2026-01-01, 2026-02-01)
cursor = dlt.sources.incremental(
    "created_at",
    initial_value=pendulum.datetime(2026, 1, 1, tz="UTC"),
    end_value=pendulum.datetime(2026, 2, 1, tz="UTC"),
)
rows = dataset.table("events").incremental(cursor).fetchall()
```

```py
rows = dataset.table("events", incremental=cursor).fetchall()
```

### Simple Arrow transformation with dlt pipeline

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/dlt-ecosystem/transformations/pandas

Creates a new table from an existing user table, selecting only non-private columns. Uses the `iter_arrow()` method on the relation to iterate over Arrow tables in chunks instead of fetching all at once.

```python
pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
    pipeline_name="users_pipeline",
    destination="duckdb",
    dataset_name="users_raw",
    dev_mode=True
)

# get user relation with only a few columns selected, but omitting email and name
users = pipeline.dataset().table("users").select("age", "amount_spent", "country")

# load the data into a new table called users_clean in the same dataset
pipeline.run(users.iter_arrow(chunk_size=1000), table_name="users_clean")
```

### Join new input against existing output with schema.is_new

Source: https://dlthub.com/docs/hub/transformations.md

A transformation that reads the dataset it writes to by passing the output dataset as an argument. On the first run the output has no tables yet, so guard the reference with `schema.is_new` and build the output from the source; on later runs append only users not already present using an anti-join.

```python
@dlt.hub.transformation(table_name="known_users", write_disposition="append")
def known_users(crm: dlt.Dataset, out: dlt.Dataset) -> Any:
    users = crm["users"].to_ibis()
    if out.schema.is_new:
        # first run: the output has no tables yet, so build it from the source
        yield users
    else:
        # later runs: append only users not already present in the output
        existing = out["known_users"].to_ibis()
        yield users.anti_join(existing, users.id == existing.id)

# pass the output dataset as an argument so the transformation can read it
known_pipeline.run(known_users(crm_pipeline.dataset(), known_pipeline.dataset()))
```
